# PART III — THE LAWS

> ### ◆ LAW I — GRAVITY
> $$G_{\mu\nu}[g_G]+\Lambda g^G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T^{(g)}_{\mu\nu}\qquad\text{on }B_{\rm grav},\qquad\Lambda=1/\ell^2\ \text{(static arena benchmark)}.$$
> **Full-meridian source law [v34.0; S/O].** Physical matter is distributed on $\mathcal M^5$, and the source on $B_{\rm grav}^4$ is an action-derived reduction over the **whole fiber** $L_b=q^{-1}(b)$, including both regular arcs and any required pole/core term. For a suitably specified bulk stress tensor $\mathcal T_{AB}$, horizontal tensor projection $\mathcal P_{\mu\nu}{}^{AB}$, density/measure $d\mu_b$ and normalization $\mathcal J$, its *schematic regular-fiber form* is
> $$T^{(g)}_{\mu\nu}(b)=\int_{L_b^{\rm reg}}\!\mathcal J(x)\,\mathcal P_{\mu\nu}{}^{AB}(x)\mathcal T_{AB}(x)\,d\mu_b(x)+T^{(g),\rm core}_{\mu\nu}(b).$$
> **Not yet a completed tensorial pushforward.** The measure, normalization, horizontal lift/projection, distributional core and stress conservation $\nabla_G^\mu T^{(g)}_{\mu\nu}=0$ must be derived from one covariant parent action, rather than chosen to fit Einstein solutions. *(v34.1, R59.)* Precisely: $T^{(g)}_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g_G}}\,\delta S_{\rm source}/\delta g_G^{\mu\nu}$ with $S_{\rm source}$ the **complete** non-gravitational action — matter, the meridian variable, the fiber/vertical geometric data, constraints and the core — varied at fixed independent variables; its conservation follows from the covariance of $S_{\rm source}$ together with the complete equations of motion, and *not* from fiber integration alone (§XXIX.11). If the metric dependence of $q$ or of the fiber data is substituted before varying, the chain-rule convention must be stated; it is not interchangeable with varying them independently. A regular-fiber integral is how this response is *expressed* in a chosen model; its measure and tensor comparison follow from that model. Any cover-lift integral equal to twice the base integral is a covering identity, not two copies of matter. The meridian structure that selects the fiber and the source that is reduced along it are varied **consistently**, core contributions included: Law I and Law II are one variational problem. On each regular meridian, the pullback of the base Einstein residual constrains the middle-space fields **horizontally**, with no independent metric equation for its vertical direction. Only if $\mathcal T$ is distributionally supported at the two bisection crossings does the above reduction specialize—with correct weights—to the old $\sum_{x\in(q\circ\iota)^{-1}(b)}$ rule. Neither twin symmetry nor a double cover authorizes counting one physical source twice. No propagating meridian radion is implied merely by taking an integral. The base-to-representational optical metric and observable map remain open **[O]**.

> **Action formulation and status [S/O].** The target is a diffeomorphism-compatible parent variational problem $S_{\rm parent}[\Psi_{\mathcal M},\mathcal C,q,g_G;\dots]$ with a variationally defined reduced stress tensor and an effective base action whose metric Euler–Lagrange equation is the Einstein equation above. Equivalently, $q^*(G[g_G]+\Lambda g_G-8\pi GT^{(g)}/c^4)=0$ is a **horizontal** constraint on the regular middle space (the pullback $q^*g_G$ is degenerate in meridian directions), not five-dimensional GR. The geometric/topological quotient is known in the static pencil away from poles; the physical source reduction and the parent action are **not yet constructed**. Varying $G$ or deriving it from middle-space mass content is an additional open macroscopic Machian program, not a derivation from the existing closure identity.

> ### ◆ LAW II — THE MERIDIANS
> The middle space carries a one-dimensional **meridian structure** $U_{\rm mer}$, regular as a foliation away from controlled singular sets. (In the static limit it is a *pencil*: distinct meridians meet at the poles, so it is not a foliation of all of $S^4$ — §VIII.1.) The representational base resolves its representatives; gravity quotients it. In the static spherical limit it must reduce to the great circles of $S^4$ through both poles, with quotient $\mathbb{RP}^3$. The general equation selecting the meridian structure is **open** **[O]**.
>
> **v34.1 — what the dominant-primary branch must contain, and the acceptance condition (R60–R61).** *(i) The exterior seed (Entries 156–158, 30 September; §XXII.12).* The intended primary-centred geometry never required the meridians to meet at a point. A finite, matter-conditioned **interlocking interior** $\mathcal I$ with a smooth transition $\mathcal T$ to an exterior $\mathcal E\ni S^3_{\rm rep}$ is the physical candidate; the round point-pencil is its **zero-core limit**. The gravitational seed uses only three *exterior* conditions: **(A)** the meridian tangent has small projection onto the selected $S^3$ (normal crossing; exact for the round pencil), **(B)** the neighbouring-meridian congruence, measured by its Jacobi map and expansion, is organized as an inward radial pencil — which is *not* a tangent radial vector on the leaf, that being a separate derived readout — and **(C)** a meridian entering the interior from one crossing returns near the antipodal crossing, with a defined return map and a quantified deviation. Nothing is demanded of the meridians *inside* the core. *(ii) The acceptance condition.* Law II must be universal and responsive to all physical middle-space matter, but its solutions must exhibit dominance by configuration and scale: one overwhelmingly dominant concentration establishes the global or regional meridian organization; much smaller bodies perturb it without each generating an independent global pencil or a homogeneous base source. Under the coupled Law I–Law II system a secondary must retain its localized reduced stress and recover the Newtonian $1/r$ potential and $v^2=G_{\rm eff}m/r$ nearby, *including* the secondary-induced change of the meridian field, not only in the frozen-pencil approximation; $\delta T^{(g)}=D_{\mathcal T}\mathscr R[\delta\mathcal T]+D_q\mathscr R[\delta q]$, and the second term must neither smear nor cancel the first (first executed step: §XXIX.12). The primary-to-uniform-source mechanism must be traced to the primary's core geometry and its distribution of matter over meridian directions, never applied to every concentration. Strong local gradients of a small body are permitted; a separate $G_{\rm secondary}$ is not. Failure to preserve localized Keplerian gravity under meridian backreaction falsifies the proposed Law II. *(iii) Branch symmetry.* The law is to be written on the parent package without an electron/neutrino label (§XXII.11, §XXIX.14); the accessible rendering is selected by the solution.

> ### ◆ STRUCTURE III — THE CANONICAL CONNECTION
> *Defined on the regular stratum $E^\circ$; its Chern class lives on linking spheres in the regular complement, where the circle acts freely (§II.2).*
>
> *Numbered III for continuity with earlier versions, but **not a law**: there is no field equation here, and calling it one would misdescribe the document's own architecture.*
> The canonical fiber carries a connection $\mathcal{A}_H$ with curvature $F_H = d\mathcal{A}_H$. Its **topological type is fixed by the spin geometry**: every relevant linking shell carries a unit class, $|c_1| = 1$, with total space $S^3$. The **sign** is induced globally — by the chosen orientation, the embedding, and the restriction map — and is neither chosen shell by shell nor set by whether matter is present; in particular, a single meridian's two crossings carry *opposite* induced signs, while with several meridians only the total over all crossings is forced to vanish (§V.4). It is independent of the source's mass and of any parameter. The reference connection is the canonical Hopf connection, and deformations away from it leave $c_1$ untouched, since $\int_{S^2}d\alpha = 0$. *(v34.1 convention, R75: the connection one-form is normalized so that $\vartheta(\xi) = 1$ on the fundamental vertical field of the period-$2\pi$ circle action, and the class is $c_1 = (2\pi)^{-1}\int_{S^2}F_H = \pm1$; vector-valued wedge notation can hide a factor two, and the Berry and real-Hopf conventions used in Parts XXIV–XXVIII are to be read against this normalization.)* In an adapted metric they appear as **two local connection cross-components**, whose gauge-invariant content is fixed only after quotienting the $U(1)$ gauge freedom $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$ (§III.3). **Nothing in this version sources them, and no matter-coupling law is asserted** **[O]**.

> ### ◆ LAW IV — ELECTROMAGNETISM
> Maxwell on $B_{\rm rep}$, with $\epsilon = \mu_{\rm EM} = 1$. Light resolves meridian representatives and does **not** perform the gravity quotient. The field lives downstairs, so its pullback to $E$ is **$U(1)_H$-invariant** — it does not couple to the fiber. (Earlier drafts called it a "zero mode," which implies a Kaluza–Klein expansion this version does not perform; see §XI.1.) *(v34.1 type correction, R72.)* An embedding $\iota:B_{\rm rep}\hookrightarrow\mathcal M$ supplies no map $E\to B_{\rm rep}$, so a field on $B_{\rm rep}$ pulls back only to the restricted bundle $E_{\rm rep}=\pi_H^{-1}(B_{\rm rep})$, not to all of $E$; an extension to $E$ needs a further map or extension rule, and the equatorial $S^3$ is not a retract of $S^4$ (a regular-stratum retraction fails at the poles). Under the full-middle-space ontology the four-dimensional Dirac and Maxwell actions of this document are **proposed effective readout actions, or explicitly leaf-supported sectors**; their relation to physical middle-space fields and to the reduced gravitational source is open and is not settled by the blanket conditional note. Invariance under the circle action is also not independence of the fiber geometry: a circle-neutral mode still contributes fiber-length-dependent stress through the measure and kinetic term (Toy B).

The epistemic architecture, at a glance:

**Law II restated, with its coupling to Law I (v34.0; the author's clarification of 11 October) [S/O].** *What Law II is.* A universal, matter-coupled **meridian-equilibrium law**: a one-dimensional line distribution $U_{\rm mer}\subset T\mathcal M$ on the regular stratum of the middle space, represented locally by $u^A$ up to nonzero rescaling and sign, selected by the *entire* middle-space matter configuration through a covariant stationarity condition — schematically $\delta S_{\rm mer}[u,H,\Psi_{\mathcal M},\ldots]/\delta u = 0$ with its regularity, line-field gauge and constraints specified — whose integral leaves define the quotient $q:\mathcal M\to B_{\rm grav}$ where a Hausdorff leaf space exists, with the singular (pole/core) stratum resolved separately. Its source may involve middle-space stress, currents, spectral or compatibility data, or an order parameter built from them; it may not involve a hand-inserted label "primary". *What a primary is.* A concentration that dominates the selection operator over a substantial domain and range of scales, $\mathcal D_i = \{p:\text{centre }i\text{ dominates the Law II response at }p\}$ once the operator, norm and measure are specified — relational and domain-relative (a primary for one domain is a secondary for a larger one), never a species, threshold or rank. *What the static pencil is.* The great-circle pencil of §VIII.1 with its common poles is the intended **dominant-mass solution branch** for $n = 1$, to be *derived* as the stationary configuration when one concentration dominates; it is presently assumed there, and Law II is the law that must explain when and why that branch occurs. *Primary dominance without rigidity.* With $\Psi = \Psi_{\rm prim}+\epsilon\Psi_{\rm sec}$ and a justified smallness norm, $U = U_0[\Psi_{\rm prim}]+\epsilon\,\delta U[\Psi_{\rm sec}]+O(\epsilon^2)$ away from the secondary's own neighbourhood and from degeneracies of the selection operator — background-dominating meridian orientation *plus* locally responsive gravity, not dominant matter owning the fibers and erasing other sources; the secondary's full-fiber Law I reduction must give its ordinary local field, $\Phi_{\rm sec}\simeq-G_{\rm eff}M_{\rm sec}/r$, $v^2_{\rm circ}\simeq G_{\rm eff}M_{\rm sec}/r$ for $r\ll\ell$, with no order-one fifth force. *Radiality, typed.* At the equatorial leaf $\theta = \pi/2$ the great-circle tangent $\partial_\theta X = -p$ is normal to the leaf; "meridians moving radially through a leaf" is therefore *extrinsic radial passage* through the surrounding $S^4$, transverse to the $S^3$ leaves (what the pencil realizes), while any *intrinsic radial direction on a leaf toward a represented mass* is an additional derived readout — the gradient of the reduced base potential pulled back to the leaf, for instance — and the two are not to be identified by calling a normal vector radial. *Coupling to Law I.* Because the fibers respond to matter, the source map is a functional of the dynamically selected quotient, $T^{(g)} = \mathscr R_{q[u,\Psi,\ldots]}[\mathcal T,\Psi,H,\ldots]$, and its first variation carries $D_q\mathscr R[\delta q]$, measure, core and connection terms beside $D_{\mathcal T}\mathscr R[\delta\mathcal T]$; Law I's metric and matter may not be varied while Law II's fiber map is held fixed except in a named fixed-meridian approximation (the regime of every static calculation in Parts IV–XXV). *Many primaries.* For $n$ separated primary-sized concentrations in a middle space with $L_{\rm middle}\gg a_i$, the same law should select a locally primary-centred germ with its own $S^3$-type readout around each, with transition strata between basins; the output of Law II must then be one of — a single singular line distribution with composable leaves, a stratified foliation with transition strata, an atlas of local quotient charts with a gluing theorem, or something else to be named — and the physical source on overlaps pushed forward exactly once. Permutation-equivariance under relabelling of centres is required; no parameter of the law may depend on $n$ or on the identity of the strongest centre. The round $S^4(\ell)$ with its equatorial $S^3(\ell)$ does not realize $L_{\rm middle}\gg a_i$ and is the $n = 1$ benchmark only. *Status.* Intention and construction target; the topological pencil and its $\mathbb{RP}^3$ quotient and $S^3$ bisection are derived *given* the pencil (§VIII.1), its selection by matter, the leaf radiality, the pole dynamics and generic quotient regularity are not. The table above is read accordingly: Law II's row records the sought law, the historical "sourced by the primary's degeneracies" being the $n = 1$ branch described from its solution.

## III.2 Law I locks the fiber length [S]

In the conformal/static sector, with $g_{\rm spatial} = \Omega^2g_{\rm ref}$ and $\Omega = \phi^2$:

$$L_H = \Omega\,L_H^{\rm ref},\qquad\text{so to first order}\qquad \frac{\delta L_H}{L_H} = -\Phi$$

> **Scope [D], new in 17.6.** This locking holds on the regular stratum $E^\circ$. Near a restored meridian a smooth completion forces $L_H\to0$ (§II.2), so the locking cannot hold all the way to a source: it gives way inside a collapse core, as the Taub–NUT fiber does, or the metric on $E$ is singular there.

> **To first order, the fiber-length increase tracks the Newtonian potential**, and space stretches as much as time slows. The qualifier is not decorative: the relation parts company with Schwarzschild at $O(m^2/r^2)$, as the scope box below shows.

> **Gravity does not create the fiber — the spin geometry supplies it (Part I). Gravity determines its metric size.**

**The direction, stated carefully [D/O].** The defensible relation is **one-way**:

$$g_G\ \longmapsto\ L_H = \mathcal{F}[g_G]$$

Law I solves the base geometry; the canonical metric is then constrained so that its fiber length records part of that solution.

> **A two-way relation would be much stronger, and is not claimed.** $g_G$ is a metric; $L_H$ is a single scalar function. One scalar cannot in general reconstruct four-dimensional geometry — this document itself separately carries a lapse $N$, a conformal factor $\phi$, and a meridian scale $\kappa$ (§IV.5). A statement $L_H\Leftrightarrow g_G$ would hold only in a restricted one-function sector, and no such sector has been isolated here **[O]**.

**And the future emergence claim is a different one.** If an action is later exhibited in which varying the *full* canonical metric yields Einstein's equation downstairs, what that would establish is

$$\hat g\ \Longrightarrow\ g_G$$

**not** $L_H\Rightarrow g_G$. The six-dimensional metric carries far more than its fiber length, and conflating the two would claim emergence from a scalar that only emergence from the whole metric could support. That distinction is likely to matter later.

*Scope.* This is a first-order statement. Isotropic Schwarzschild has $N = (1-m/2r)/(1+m/2r)$ while $N = \Omega^{-1}$ would require $(1+m/2r)^{-2}$; expanding, $1-m/r+m^2/2r^2$ against $1-m/r+3m^2/4r^2$ — they agree to first order and part at $O(m^2/r^2)$, with $N\Omega = 1-m^2/4r^2$ **[V]**. Imposing $N\Omega = 1$ exactly gives the Majumdar–Papapetrou form and hence extremal Reissner–Nordström, $Q = M$ — every body an extremal black hole, **excluded** **[V/T]** as a *universal* condition. As a *characterization* it is exact: $N\Omega = 1$ holds precisely for extremal holes (§X.2). Deriving the locking from an action, rather than imposing it, is open **[O]**.

## III.3 The metric-component decomposition, on the physical real shell [V/S]

A metric on the three-manifold $S^3$ has $3\cdot4/2 = 6$ components. Adapted to the circle bundle $S^3\to S^2$ they decompose as below. **This is a block count of metric components, not of physical propagating degrees of freedom** — gauge and diffeomorphism freedom would have to be removed for that, and is not:

| block | count | content |
|:--|--:|:--|
| shell 2-metric | 3 | the base geometry, from Law I |
| fiber length $L_H$ | 1 | the gravitational fiber scale, from Law I |
| connection cross-components | 2 | **open** — and *local components*, not gauge-invariant content |
| **total** | **6** | ✓ **[V]** |

So the attractive $3+1+2$ partition survives — **on the physical real slice**. Version 15 does not assert it for the full complex shell; the complex homogeneous bundle is the analytic parent, and the real slice is where the metric count is performed.

**Four of the six are assigned; two are not [D].** Gravity determines the shell geometry and Law I locks the fiber length to it — that is the $3+1$. The remaining $2$ are **left open**, deliberately.

> Earlier versions assigned those two to the odd matter sector, $T_-\to2$. **That assignment is retired** (§XI.1) — it was made because there happened to be two of them, which is not a reason.
>
> **A stronger claim would be wrong, and is not made.** A connection may vary freely while its class stays fixed: under $F\mapsto F+d\alpha$ with $\alpha$ a global 1-form, $\int_{S^2}d\alpha = 0$ by Stokes, so $c_1$ is untouched **[T]**. Connections form an affine space over the 1-forms, all sharing one class. **So fixed $c_1$ does not forbid connection dynamics.** What it forbids is specifically the old *integrated flux law* $c_1\propto M_-/m_{\rm unit}$, which made the class itself mass-dependent. The position here is simply that **the connection is unsourced and its deformations unassigned** — no impossibility claim is needed or made.

The two are **local connection cross-components** of an adapted metric, not two physical degrees of freedom: a $U(1)$ connection on an $S^2$ patch has two local components, but $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$ is gauge, and the gauge-invariant content is fixed only after that freedom is quotiented. The same discipline applies here as to the six above. They may remain unassigned until the theory itself says what they do.

# PART IV — IDENTITIES AND THEOREMS

> ### ◆ A NOTE ON THE TAGS IN THIS PART
> Every result below was verified or derived **in the architecture of versions 6 through 14**. They are stated in full because they are the theory's content, but within version 15 they carry the tag **[C]** — *conditional on the static regression of §VIII.1*. Where a bracket below reads $[V]$ or $[D]$, it records the status of the original computation, not a claim that the result has been re-established here. **Exceptions, new in the version-16 draft and tagged on their own:** the cover–quotient mass lemma in §IV.2, the pointer in §IV.7, the flag in §IV.10, and the galactic material in §IV.8.
>
> **What the condition amounts to.** §VIII.1 splits the static limit into two parts: an **assumption [S]** that the meridian structure is the antipodal great-circle pencil, and a **derivation [D]** that such a pencil has quotient $\mathbb{RP}^3$. *The static limit as a whole is therefore not derived* — only its quotient is, and only given the pencil. Everything below is conditional on the assumption as well as on the remaining regression steps.

## IV.1 The twin theorem, restated on the gravity base [V/T]

The static operator is $\Delta+3$, and Law I poses it on the spatial gravity slice $\Sigma_{\rm grav}\equiv\mathbb{RP}^3(\ell)$ of $B_{\rm grav}^{\rm static}\simeq\mathbb{R}_t\times\Sigma_{\rm grav}$, whose functions are the antipodally *even* functions on the double cover $\Sigma_{\rm rep}\equiv S^3(\ell)$. On $S^3$ the degree-$n$ harmonics have $\Delta = -n(n+2)$ and parity $(-1)^n$, so the kernel of $\Delta+3$ is exactly the degree-one dipoles — and those are **odd**. Hence

$$\ker\big(\Delta_{\Sigma_{\rm grav} }+3\big) = 0$$

and every source on the gravity base has a static solution **[T]**. Under $\pi:\Sigma_{\rm rep}\to\Sigma_{\rm grav}$ a point source $\delta_b$ lifts to $\pi^*\delta_b = \delta_x+\delta_{-x}$, which is automatically orthogonal to every dipole **[V]**.

> **One projective source downstairs is one same-sign antipodal pair on the cover.** The twin is not forced by solvability. It is what a single gravitational source on $\mathbb{RP}^3$ looks like when lifted to the resolved $S^3$ — the seed's sentence, *light resolves a representative; gravity resolves a class*, in its most literal form.

The older argument posed the operator on $S^3$ itself, where a lone pole has a nonzero dipole — a ball at the pole has $0.169$ — and a numerical solve returns the kernel mode as its symptom. That computation survives as a **consistency check**: an unsymmetrized source on the cover does not descend to the gravity base. The Green's functions, the twin's same-sign well and the plateau of §IV.8 are unchanged, since every one of them was computed with the lifted, symmetric source.

## IV.2 Closure and the $G$ identity [D]

**v34.0 pointer.** §XXIX.9 proves that under the geometric disintegration of the great-circle pencil any distribution axisymmetric about the common poles — in particular a primary concentrated at a pole, the "centre of the space enclosed by the representational three-sphere" of Entry 257, invisible to leaf readouts — reduces to a *uniform* source on $\mathbb{RP}^3$ of the same total mass. The Einstein-static closure source is therefore realizable, within the corrected Law I and *if* the geometric measure is the physical one, as the reduction of a pole-concentrated primary of mass $M_{\rm grav} = M_c/2$ — a **candidate** for what $M_c$ is, tested in §XXIX.9, and not an identification: the measure, the primary's stresses and the Keplerian secondary all have to pass the tests listed there.

The gravity base is the Einstein static universe: $\Lambda = 1/\ell^2$, $\bar\rho_{\rm geom}\equiv G\bar\rho_{\rm mass}/c^2 = 1/4\pi\ell^2$. The meridian flux through every latitude is $M_c$, and closure fixes it:

$$\frac{GM_c}{c^2\ell} = \frac{\pi}{2}$$

**A constraint on the particular Einstein-static benchmark, not a derivation of either $G$ or a microscopic/meridian mass definition.** The apparent Schwarzschild-radius comparison does not establish a horizon. In v34.0 the natural physical question is whether a separately computed *full-meridian middle-space mass/response functional*, reduced by the new Law I, can reproduce the required closure source without postulating it. No particular candidate for that functional is adopted.

> **Lifted and quotient masses — a lemma [T], new in the version-16 draft.** Let $\pi:\Sigma_{\rm rep}\to\Sigma_{\rm grav}$ — that is, $S^3(\ell)\to\mathbb{RP}^3(\ell)$ — be the double cover. A gravity-base source of mass $m$ at $b$ lifts to $\pi^*\delta_b = \delta_x+\delta_{\tau x}$, with coefficient $m$ at each preimage, so
> $$\int_{\Sigma_{\rm rep} }\pi^*\rho_g\;=\;2\int_{\Sigma_{\rm grav} }\rho_g$$
> **Cover, base, and middle-space masses — revised status.** The exact geometric covering statement $M_{\rm lift}=2M_{\rm grav}$ refers to the **integral of the pulled-back base source**, not to twice the physical matter. Define three distinct concepts: $M_{\rm mid}$, the yet-to-be-defined physical middle-space matter/response content, involving a full-meridian reduction and operational energy normalization; $M_{\rm grav}$, the integral of the effective source on $\mathbb{RP}^3$; and $M_{\rm lift}=2M_{\rm grav}$, the mathematical pullback integral on the covering $S^3$. A fourth, $M_{\rm instance}$, characterizes matter accessible in one representational localization. **No general equality $M_{\rm mid}=M_{\rm grav}=M_{\rm instance}$ is established**; there is no generic factor two between physical and gravitational mass. The previously reported $M_{\rm rep}=M_{\rm grav}$ for a point source depends on the former two-point-supported source model. The closure variable $M_c$ is, in the old Einstein-static calculation, $M_{\rm lift}$; its possible origin as a full-middle-space mass or collective response is now a distinct open identification, not a definition imposed in advance.

## IV.3 Law I as the fiber-length equation [V]

Weak-field statics are conformally round, and the Hamiltonian constraint linearizes to

$$(\Delta_{S^3}+3)\,\delta\phi = -2\pi\,\delta\rho_+$$

the twin-theorem operator acting on the conformal factor. For a ball with its twin, $\phi^2 = 2.017$ at the ball's center and identically at the **empty** twin, agreeing to $10^{-11}$ **[V]**.

## IV.4 Weyl from the fiber length [V/D]

Wherever the stress is isotropic — vacuum, the arena constant, a static fluid — the electric Weyl tensor of a static solution is the trace-free Ricci tensor of its spatial metric, $E_{ij} = [R_{ij}(h)]^{\rm TF} = [N^{-1}D_iD_jN]^{\rm TF}$. For this theory's slices, $h = \phi^4g_{\rm ref}$ with $\phi = \sqrt{L_H/2\pi\ell}$, the reference Ricci tensor is pure trace and drops out, leaving the **exact** relation, in an orthonormal frame,

$$E_{\hat i\hat j} = \phi^{-4}\Big[-2\phi^{-1}\nabla_i\nabla_j\phi+6\phi^{-2}\nabla_i\phi\,\nabla_j\phi\Big]^{\rm TF}$$

with $\nabla$ the reference derivative **[D]**. The gradient term is genuinely nonlinear. In the weak field it drops out, leaving

$$E_{ij}\simeq-2\big[\nabla_i\nabla_j\phi\big]^{\rm TF}$$

whose trace-free Hessian is the tidal field, while the Hessian's trace is the matter. For Schwarzschild, $\phi = 1+m/2r$, the exact eigenvalues are $(m/R^3)(-2,1,1)$ in the areal radius $R = r\phi^2$ — radial stretching, transverse squeezing — and the linear formula gives the same pattern in the isotropic radius **[V]**, checked symbolically together with $E_{ij} = N^{-1}D_iD_jN$. The field is Petrov type D, with repeated principal null directions along $\partial_t\pm\widehat{\nabla L_H}$, the directions of steepest fiber-length change. *An earlier revision quoted $(m/r^3)(1,-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$, which are the eigenvalues of $[\nabla\nabla\phi]^{\rm TF}$ itself, not of $E$ — off by a factor of $-2$ — and presented the linear formula as exact* **[R]**.
## IV.5 The metric, written out [V/D]

$$ds^2 = -N^2dt^2 + L_H^2\big(d\theta+\alpha\big)^2 + \kappa^2du^2 + \phi^4g_{S^3}$$

with $N$ and $L_H$ from Law I, $\alpha$ the connection of Structure III, $u$ the meridian and $\kappa$ its scale. *(v34.1 normalization, R75: with $\theta$ of period $2\pi$ the coefficient that gives the fiber circumference $L_H$ is $(L_H/2\pi)^2$; the form displayed is correct for a period-one fiber coordinate, which is the convention adopted here.)* For a point mass, with $M\equiv M_{\rm grav}$ the local gravity-base source (§IV.2), $\phi = 1 + GM/2r + O(r^2/\ell^2)$, and near the source the four-dimensional part is **isotropic Schwarzschild, as the $R/\ell\ll1$ local comparison solution** **[C]**:

$$ds^2_4 = -\left(\frac{1-GM/2r}{1+GM/2r}\right)^2dt^2 + \left(1+\frac{GM}{2r}\right)^4\big(dr^2+r^2d\Omega_2^2\big)$$

with closure corrections at $O(r^2/\ell^2)$ — about $6\%$ at 10 kpc in the galactic arena ($\ell = 16$ kpc), negligible on planetary scales; the old $4\times10^{-15}$ belonged to the retired cosmological $\ell = 63$ Gpc. Shells have proper area $4\pi r^2(1+GM/2r)^4$. The meridian scale $\kappa$ remains undetermined **[O]**.

## IV.6 Black holes [T/C]

Nothing in this version adds a charge to a black hole. As **local comparison solutions**, valid for $R/\ell\ll1$, a neutral secondary has the Schwarzschild exterior on the gravity base and a charged one Reissner–Nordström,

$$f(r) = 1 - \frac{2GM}{c^2r} + \frac{Gq^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0c^4r^2}$$

with $q$ the ordinary SI charge and no additional contribution — in the geometrized units of Part X, $G = c = 4\pi\epsilon_0 = 1$, simply $1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2$, with $M^2\geq Q^2$ for a hole. The exact black hole of the closed arena, with its constant $\Lambda = \ell^{-2}$ and its closure source, is open (§X.10).

> Earlier versions carried a second charge $P = g_2M/m_{\rm unit}$, built from the flux sector, which tightened extremality to $M^2\geq Q^2+P^2$ universally and was bounded by Mercury at $g_2/m_{\rm unit}<0.024$. **All of that is retired** (§XI.1): with the fiber's Chern class fixed at $\pm1$ by spin geometry, there is no mass-proportional flux to gravitate and no parameter to bound.

## IV.7 Charge and the twin [V/D]

*v34.0 supersession note.* "The seed puts nothing at the twin" is the leaf-supported special model: under the corrected Law I (Part III; §§XXIX.8–9) the twin is an empty *readout* of a class whose complete meridian may carry matter, and the Maxwell field's placement along the fiber is open; the local Coulomb computations stand as calculations in the former model.

Gauss on a closed section forces a compensating charge somewhere, and the seed puts nothing at the twin. With the compensator wherever the other charges are, the field of a charge $Q$ is regular at the twin and vanishes there — verified, $|E|\to0$ **linearly**. **The twin carries gravitational shape with no electromagnetic content**; a charged secondary's twin holds the $Q^2/r^2$ term as a *tidal* charge with $\nabla\cdot E = 0$ and $E = 0$. *Within the summed-source architecture this barrenness is strongly constrained: since gravity sums over sheets, field energy duplicated at the twin would add to active but not passive mass, and lunar laser ranging bounds the duplicated fraction at $\eta\lesssim5\times10^{-11}$ (§X.13, under the assumptions stated there).*

## IV.8 Orbits and the $v^2$ family [V]

On the gravity base a secondary is a well in the jellium, and closed-universe orbits are retrograde-precessing rosettes: apsidal advance $1.945\pi$ per radial period at small apocenter, falling to $1.836\pi$ mid-disk. The kinematic pattern speed $\Omega-\kappa/2$ falls by a factor 10 across a disk where Kepler alone gives 20 — **the closure term halves the winding rate of kinematic spirals.**

For circular orbits at colatitude $\chi$, $v^2(\chi) = \Phi'(\chi)\tan\chi$, and at the equator $\Phi'(\pi/2) = 0$ by twin symmetry, so $v^2_{\rm eq} = -\Phi''(\pi/2)$. Solving for a lump holding a fraction $f$ of the closure mass gives, converged as the lump shrinks,

$$v^2_{\rm eq} = 2.352\,f = 1.497\,\frac{GM_{\rm lift} }{\ell} = 2.994\,\frac{GM_{\rm grav} }{\ell}$$

**independent of how the lump is packed** — only the monopole survives at the equator. *(v34.1 scope, R65.)* For a static spherical metric with areal radius $R(x)$ the circular speed is $v^2=RN'/(NR')$; at a reflection-symmetric equator both derivatives vanish and the *continuation of neighbouring circular orbits* has the limit $v^2\to RN''/(NR'')|_{\rm eq}$, provided $R''\neq0$ and the limit is timelike; $-N''/N$ uses the round relation $R''=-R$ and is valid to first perturbative order, not as an exact identity for the perturbed areal radius $R=\phi^2\sin x$. At the exact symmetric equator the radial geodesic condition is $0=0$ and selects no unique speed: the plateau is the limit of a selected family of nearby orbits, a finite endpoint value on a bounded areal-radius interval, which is weaker than an observed extended flat curve (§XXIX.13). *(v30 correction, §XXV.2: the coefficient is the analytic $3$, with $2\sqrt2$ at the $\pi/4$ dip — $v^2/c^2 = \mu(\csc\chi+2\sin\chi)$ — and the historical $2.994$, $1.497$, $1.413$ are $3$, $1.5$, $\sqrt2$ to $0.2\%$; the calculation is the scalar solver's benchmark, and the physical rotation curve is derived from the full first-order equations under the rigid-closure premise in §XXV.5, where the point source gives $2.977\,\mu$ and an extended galaxy less.)* *(Earlier quotations of this coefficient mixed the two mass conventions; they are recorded in §XI.1.)*

**Extended profiles: the shape family [V].** For an exponential profile $\rho\propto e^{-\chi/h}$ about the pole, with its same-sign twin, the curve keeps its characteristic shape — a peak, a fall, a shallow dip, and a rise to a *nonzero* equatorial plateau — with the family parametrized by $h/\ell$:

| $h/\ell$ | peak $v^2$ (at $\chi$) | dip $v^2$ (at $\chi$) | equatorial $v^2$ |
|--:|:--|:--|--:|
| 0.01 | 9.73 (0.034) | 1.413 (0.785) | 1.498 |
| 0.03 | 3.32 (0.104) | 1.406 (0.785) | 1.492 |
| 0.10 | — rising, then a flat shoulder | — | 1.417 |
| 0.30 | — monotone rise | — | 0.923 |

all in units of $GM/\ell$. For compact profiles the dip sits at $\chi = \pi/4$, about 6% below the plateau, and the equatorial value tends to $1.497$; for broad ones the peak and dip disappear and the equatorial value falls. So "packing-independent" holds in the compact limit $h\ll\ell$, not for profiles comparable to the sphere.

**The intended arena is galactic [V/S/O].** The plateau lives at the scale $\ell$, and the intended reading is a *galactic* three-sphere — not a cosmological one.

> **Which mass.** Below, $M_{\rm gal}\equiv M_{\rm grav}$ is the galaxy's own gravitational mass, so a compact source gives $v^2_{\rm eq} = 2.994\,GM_{\rm gal}/\ell$; the factor of two against the lifted mass is the lemma of §IV.2, confirmed independently by a Kepler test on the near field **[V]**.

> **One arena.** Here $\ell$ is the radius of the galactic slice $\Sigma_{\rm grav} = \mathbb{RP}^3(\ell)$, and every result was computed on its double cover $\Sigma_{\rm rep} = S^3(\ell)$ with the lifted, symmetric source — which, by §IV.1, is exactly the gravity-base problem; there is no second, cosmological scale to confuse it with. What remains open is the arena's background: at galactic $\ell$ the Einstein-static relations demand a uniform closure source that Law I's source map does not yet generate (the closure row below; §XI.2, item 0′). If that background is ever replaced, the linear operator — and with it the coefficient $2.994$ — must be re-derived **[O]**.

At galactic scale the plateau is then of the right *order*. A compact $6\times10^{10}M_\odot$ gives $v\approx311$ km/s at $\ell = 8$ kpc and 220 km/s at 16 kpc. The Milky Way's own profile, taken **isotropically** on the sphere with its exponential scale $h = 2.6$ kpc, gives $235$ km/s at 8 kpc and $205$ km/s at 16 kpc, and **reaches 220 km/s at $\ell\approx13$ kpc** **[V]**. The model keeps this isotropic treatment deliberately, as the conservative choice; a thin-disk geometry enters only the detached wing (Part XII). Under the arena law of the detached wing (Part XII), the Milky Way's $\ell$ would be $25$ kpc and its plateau $175$ km/s, matching MOND's asymptotic value for the same baryons — a wing result, not a claim of the model.

Four things stand between this and a galactic theory:

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **a law for $\ell$** | the model has one arena, the Milky Way's, and nothing yet fixes its radius; other galaxies' arenas are not part of the model (detached wing, Part XII) |
| **realistic profiles** | taken isotropically, the Milky Way's exponential profile ($h = 2.6$ kpc) keeps $87\%$ of the compact plateau at $\ell = 16$ kpc and reaches 220 km/s at $\ell\approx13$ kpc **[V]**. Broader profiles lose the plateau quickly; the thin-disk alternative, which holds it better, is confined to the detached wing (Part XII) |
| **the sphere cannot be the space we see** | on a sphere of radius $\ell$, angular-diameter distances are $\ell\sin\chi\leq\ell$. At $\ell\approx16$ kpc GRAVITY's geometric $R_0 = 8.18$ kpc fits, but the LMC at 49.6 kpc exceeds the cap 3 times, Leo I at 254 kpc 16 times and M31 at 765 kpc 48 times; light would also circle the sphere in $3\times10^5$ yr, giving the galaxy repeated images of itself. So **if light uses $r^*g_G$, as §V.1 says, the galactic $S^3$ dies observationally**. The alternative — an optical sector that departs from $r^*g_G$ globally, matching it only locally — needs new structure, and must still reproduce lensing, which sees the same mass discrepancy that dynamics does (§XI.2, item 0) |
| **closure at galactic scale** | at $\ell\approx16$ kpc the **assumed Einstein-static base solution** demands $M_{\rm lift}\approx5.3\times10^{17}M_\odot$ (base-equivalent $M_{\rm grav}\approx2.6\times10^{17}M_\odot$), vastly exceeding the Galaxy's baryons. The new full-meridian Law I admits physical content outside the selected representational leaf as a candidate source, but **does not demonstrate** that it provides this budget, nor exempt it from conservation, optical and gravitational constraints. Whether it is physical bulk stress, a collective reduction response or an effective geometric contribution is open. The small Milky Way mass appearing when $v_{\rm eq}^2\ell/(3G)$ is evaluated is a numerical/phenomenological observation, **not** the value of $M_c$ or proof that $G$ has been derived. |

**What the galactic sphere is — such that it shapes orbits without capping distances — is the open problem (§XI.2).**

**Other galaxies: a detached wing.** The Tully–Fisher lemma, the arena law, the apparent-scale rule and the exploratory SPARC checks concern galaxies other than ours. They are deliberately **not attached** to the model and are collected in Part XII.

## IV.9 The lumped-mass limit [V/D]

Closure fixes the lifted total at $M_{\rm lift} = \pi\ell/2$ — equivalently $M_{\rm grav} = \pi\ell/4$ (§IV.2) — so a secondary holds a fraction $f$ of it, the same ratio in either convention provided numerator and denominator match. At $f = 1$ the lump's lifted-mass Schwarzschild radius is $\pi\ell$, the diameter of $S^3$; its physical near-field radius, $2GM_{\rm grav}/c^2 = \pi\ell/2$, is the diameter of the gravity base $\mathbb{RP}^3$ — **either way, the diameter of the universe.** That suggests no exterior and no orbits — but a Schwarzschild radius compared with a diameter is not a horizon, and the claim needs an actual closed-base solution before it is a theorem. Law II is untroubled: the meridian structure is intact at $f = 1$; what fails is the base geometry.

## IV.10 The Keplerian limit, quantified [V] — corrected in v30

*Correction (v30, §XXV.2): $\csc\chi$ is not the Green function of $\Delta+3$ — $(\Delta+3)\csc\chi = 4\csc\chi$ away from the poles. The even radial solution is $F(\chi) = \cos2\chi/\sin\chi = \csc\chi-2\sin\chi$, with series $1/\chi-\tfrac{11}{6}\chi+\tfrac{127}{360}\chi^3+\ldots$; the $+r^2/6\ell^2$ term below, the $6.5\%$ figure and the matching claim of §IV.5 are withdrawn. The paragraph is kept as written for the record.*

Near a point mass the Green's function goes as $1/\sin\chi$, so with $r = \ell\chi$,

$$\Phi(r) = -\frac{Gm}{r}\left[1+\frac{r^2}{6\ell^2}+O(r^4/\ell^4)\right]$$

In the galactic arena the closure correction is **about $6.5\%$ at 10 kpc** for $\ell = 16$ kpc — not a nuisance but the onset of the plateau physics of §IV.8 — and $\sim10^{-20}$ at 1 AU, so planetary dynamics are untouched. *(An earlier cosmological reading, with $\ell = 63$ Gpc, gave $4\times10^{-15}$ at 10 kpc and a "jellium crossover" at 1.2 Mpc; both figures are retired.)*

## IV.11 The static wall [T/V]

> **Identical twin wells cannot generate a relative gravitational redshift between themselves.**

A static geometry has a timelike Killing vector, so Killing energy is conserved along null geodesics and $1+z = \sqrt{g_{tt}(\text{receiver})/g_{tt}(\text{emitter})}$. When emitter and receiver sit in **identical** wells the lapses are equal and $z = 0$ identically **[V]**. Since the seed makes the twin's well identical to the source's, no shift can arise between them, and every route to Hubble's law within the static theory ends there.

*A stronger sentence carried by earlier drafts — "on a static geometry there is no redshift" — is **false** and is retired (§XI.1): Schwarzschild is static and redshifts ($z = 0.21$ from $6M$ to $100M$, $0.73$ from $3M$ to infinity)* **[V]**. *What staticity forbids is cosmological redshift from expansion, not gravitational redshift.*

# PART V — THE SEED

## V.1 Light resolves; gravity quotients [S/T]

Physical matter inhabits $\mathcal M$; the selected bisection $B_{\rm rep}$ carries the resolved matter/Maxwell/detector **readout**. An optical event is a point $x\in B_{\rm rep}$, so a representative-resolving electromagnetic sector can distinguish $x$ from $\tau x$ even if its gravitational base class is shared. The exact bulk-to-Maxwell field map is open.

Gravity uses the complete meridian quotient $q:\mathcal M\to B_{\rm grav}$; its source is reduced from the full middle-space content, while $r=q\circ\iota$ is **only** the geometry of the chosen representational bisection.

$$\text{gravity as seen on a rendering}\;=\;r^*\circ\operatorname{Einstein}\circ\mathscr R_q,\qquad \mathscr R_q:\text{middle-space source data}\to T^{(g)}\text{ on }B_{\rm grav},$$

where $\mathscr R_q$ is the **full-meridian action-compatible source-reduction operator** of Law I—not $r_*$, the old two-crossing sum. The pullback $q^*g_G$ has a meridian null direction as a bilinear form on $\mathcal M$ and is therefore **not** a five-dimensional Lorentzian metric; this expresses the horizontal character of the gravitational base constraint, not a claim that matter is confined to the bisection. As $r$ is locally a diffeomorphism away from singularities,

$$g^{(G)}_{\rm rep} = r^*g_G$$

gives a genuine Lorentzian *base-induced* metric on the selected representational leaf. Whether the physical photon/detector optical readout equals its metric optics is a separate open condition; the existing compact-optics obstruction remains.

## V.2 The barren twin, reinterpreted under full-meridian Law I [S/O; historical two-crossing demonstration retained as a limit]

A selected representational leaf may have a luminous crossing $x$ and an empty *readout* at its twin $\tau x$. The **same base geometry** pulls back to both because $q(x)=q(\tau x)$, while the base source is $\mathscr R_q[\mathcal T_{\mathcal M}]$ from the entire meridian. If physical stress is independently postulated to be supported *only* at the readout crossing $x$, the old source sum reduces to the localized instance $T^{(g)}([x])=T(x)$, with $T(\tau x)=0$. That is a **special example**, not the general source ontology; unobserved bulk matter may occupy the remaining fiber.

> **The surviving seed.** Representative-resolving matter/optical observations can distinguish two readouts of a base geometry that does not distinguish their locations. There is no theorem that the unobserved twin or the rest of the meridian contains no physical matter. Any suppression of emissions at the twin needs a separate localization/selection law.

## V.3 Why a barren twin is unobserved [V/D]

**In the historical barren-readout ansatz** it is empty of localized emitters, absorbers and scatterers; no general statement about bulk middle-space matter follows. The old twin-darkness explanation depends on an unproved selection mechanism, not on Law I itself. An earlier version added a second, causal one — the twin's light could not yet have arrived — but that belonged to the retired cosmological reading, where $\pi\ell/c = 646$ Gyr at $\ell = 63$ Gpc. In the galactic arena the crossing time is $\pi\ell/c\approx1.6\times10^5$ yr at $\ell = 16$ kpc, and light could have crossed the arena tens of thousands of times over the Galaxy's age. **If a twin readout is dark, that must follow from its matter/EM readout rule, not from remoteness or from Law I alone** — a sharper statement, with the auxiliary excuse removed.

---

## V.4 Kirchhoff at the poles: topological twin-sign pairing [T/V]

*The Hopf restrictions at the resolved crossings are globally constrained: their outward classes sum to zero. For a single meridian that forces the two crossings to carry opposite signs; for several meridians it does not pair them crossing by crossing. This section establishes exactly that, and states what it does **not** establish about where matter may sit.*

**The conservation law [T].** Alexander duality identifies a circle bundle over $S^4\setminus\Gamma$ with a 1-cycle $z = \sum_e a_e\,e$ on the graph $\Gamma$ of §II.1, where $a_e$ is the bundle's class on the small linking sphere of arc $e$. Every arc runs from pole to pole, so

$$\partial z = \Big(\sum_e a_e\Big)\big((-p)-p\big) = 0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\sum_e a_e = 0$$

The Hopf classes on the $2N$ arcs, oriented pole-outward, sum to zero: **Hopf class is conserved through the poles** — Kirchhoff's law at a vertex.

**The sign dictionary [V].** Slide each arc's linking sphere along the arc to the equator. It becomes the shell about that crossing point in $B_{\rm rep}$ with its **outward** orientation — and with the *same* sign at every crossing, since every pole-outward arc crosses the equator heading south (verified by direct orientation computation: sign $-1$ at both $\hat n$ and $-\hat n$ for pole-outward arcs, but $-1$ and $+1$ for the loop-oriented meridian). So in $B_{\rm rep}$'s own terms:

$$\sum_{\text{all }2N\text{ crossing points }x} c_{\rm out}(x) = 0$$

**The one-meridian case, checked independently [V].** Pull the Hopf bundle back along the retraction $S^4\setminus C\to S^2$, $x\mapsto(x_2,x_3,x_4)/|\cdot|$, with $C$ the meridian. On the outward shell about the source its degree is $+1$; about the twin, **$-1$**. Two independent computations, one answer: $c_{\rm out}(\hat n)+c_{\rm out}(-\hat n) = 0$.

**What is established: a sign pairing, independent of occupancy [V].**

> **The outward Hopf classes at all $2N$ crossings sum to zero.** For one meridian that is a pairing, $c_{\rm out}(\hat n) = -c_{\rm out}(-\hat n)$. For $N\geq2$ it is a single global relation, $\sum_i\big(a_{i,+}+a_{i,-}\big) = 0$, on a graph with $H_1(\Gamma)\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$, and it does **not** imply $a_{i,+} = -a_{i,-}$ for each $i$. With unit classes everywhere, Kirchhoff allows 6 sign patterns for two meridians, only 4 of them paired, and 70 for four meridians, only 16 paired **[V]**. Pairing meridian by meridian would need an additional restriction on the global bundle class, or extra geometry.

This is a property of the **global bundle, the orientation, and the restriction map** — it holds whether or not matter sits at either crossing. Accordingly Structure III is stated with $|c_1| = 1$ on every relevant linking shell and the sign *induced*, not assigned by occupancy.

**What is not established: that matter must avoid a sign [O].** An earlier draft of this section concluded that the barren twin is topologically forced. **That inference is withdrawn** (§XI.1). It ran: Part I's construction is identical at every source, so every *source* shell carries $+1$; the twin carries $-1$; so the twin cannot host a source. The middle step silently read Law 0 as fixing the **sign** at source shells relative to their outward orientation. Law 0 fixes the bundle *type* — $|c_1| = 1$, total space $S^3$ — and nothing more. Demanding the sign at source shells specifically is an **extra axiom**, and a telling one: it would make the sign at a crossing depend on whether matter sits there, so that topology would depend on matter content — precisely what the centrepiece disavows.

**An explicit counterexample [V].** Take the retraction bundle above with sources at *both* crossings of one meridian. Its outward degrees are $+1$ and $-1$; each source shell has $|c_1| = 1$, so Law 0 is satisfied at both. **A doubly occupied meridian is allowed.** What topology fixes is the pairing of signs, not the occupancy.

**What would turn pairing into barrenness.** An additional theorem or axiom of the form

$$\text{ordinary matter worldlines are compatible with only one induced Hopf sign}$$

— a **matter-selection rule**. It is not in the theory: Structure III is explicitly unsourced, with no matter coupling, so nothing currently ties matter to the sign. *Were* such a rule derived, the conclusion would follow, and it would be strong: with unit classes on every shell of the pencil, the allowed configurations would then be exactly one source and one barren twin per meridian — for **every** $N$ **[D, conditional]**. The proof is a count. Unit classes summing to zero means exactly $N$ plus signs and $N$ minus signs. Every meridian carries at least one source, and the rule puts sources on one sign only, so each of the $N$ meridians needs at least one plus; with exactly $N$ pluses, each has exactly one. Enumeration for $N\leq4$ agrees, with $2^N$ survivors — the choices of which crossing holds the source **[V]**. The pairing is *derived* here, although the global sum alone does not imply it.

**Nor is $-1$ a matter class [O].** It would be premature to say a twin could host "matter of the opposite Hopf class": nothing yet establishes that matter fields carry a Hopf-sign label at all. The prior question is whether the sign is **a property of the bundle's restriction and orientation alone, or a representation carried by a matter field**. Only the second could support a selection rule — and deriving one, rather than declaring it, would make barrenness genuinely forced, a considerably stronger result than asserting it.

**Scope.** Everything here assumes the static great-circle pencil, itself an assumption (§VIII.1), and point-like sources.

# PART VI — NEWMAN–JANIS AND KERR

## VI.1 The construction, in six steps [T/V]

**1.** Put Schwarzschild in Kerr–Schild form, $g_{ab} = \eta_{ab}+2Hk_ak_b$ with $H = M/r$ and $k$ null and geodesic for both metrics. Exact, not linearized.

**2.** Note the whole solution rests on one harmonic function: $\nabla^2(1/r) = 0$ away from the origin **[V]**.

**3.** Complexify and displace the source along the imaginary axis, $z\to z-ia$. **This step supplies the characteristic Kerr complex structure; it is not by itself the whole derivation** — see the caveat below.

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} }\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-ia)^2} }$$

still harmonic **[V]**.

**4.** The complex distance vanishes where $-2az = 0$ and $x^2+y^2+z^2 = a^2$, i.e. $z = 0$ and $x^2+y^2 = a^2$: **a ring of radius $a$** **[V]**. Schwarzschild's point singularity has become Kerr's ring.

**5.** With the oblate radius $R$ defined by $\frac{x^2+y^2}{R^2+a^2}+\frac{z^2}{R^2} = 1$, the complex distance is $R+ia\cos\theta$ and $H = MR^3/(R^4+a^2z^2)$ — **Kerr in Kerr–Schild form**.

**6.** The angular momentum is $J = Ma$, so $a = J/M$: **the imaginary displacement is the spin per unit mass.**

> ### ◆ WHAT THIS SEQUENCE DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH [T/O]
> **The complex displacement supplies the characteristic Kerr complex structure; recovery of the full metric additionally uses the Kerr–Schild null-congruence construction.** The original Newman–Janis prescription also manipulates a null tetrad and applies a *reality prescription*, and generalized Newman–Janis algorithms are known to be ambiguous away from special cases — different reality prescriptions give different metrics. The six steps above are a faithful account of the *complex-structure* content, not a self-contained derivation, and the earlier phrase "nothing is added; a source is moved" overstated that **[R]**.

## VI.2 Where this happens, and where it does not [S/D]

Newman–Janis acts on the **complexification of the representational base**:

$$B_{\rm rep}\hookrightarrow B_{ {\rm rep},\mathbb{C} }\xrightarrow{\text{shift} }B_{ {\rm rep},\mathbb{C} }\xrightarrow{\text{real slice} }B_{\rm rep}^{\rm Kerr}$$

And the canonical shells **follow the complex worldline**: at every point and radius the shell is $Q^2_{\rm aff}$ with lift $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$, so the displacement moves the center of the entire shell system. Two roles stay separate:

$$\text{Kerr rotation} = \text{complex worldline displacement},\qquad \text{the fiber} = \text{the shell's spin lift}$$

> **Rotation is not winding around the fiber.** Earlier versions tried to make one construction carry rotation, the seed, the fiber and the dynamics at once. Here complexified spacetime handles Newman–Janis, spin geometry handles the shell lift, the meridians handle the seed, and Einstein's equations handle the fiber length. **No single construction is asked to do all four jobs.**

## VI.3 The $g = 2$ signpost [T/O]

Kerr–Newman satisfies $J = Ma$ and $\mu = Qa$, hence $\mu = (Q/M)J$ — the conventional $g = 2$ relation. Complex-worldline approaches to Einstein–Maxwell give a further reason to keep the complex center visible. **A future bridge target, not a derivation of the electron.**

---

# PART VII — SPIN, AND THE CATEGORY FIREWALL

## VII.1 What the spin geometry does supply [T]

Newman–Penrose two-spinors transform under $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ — the same group that lifts the complex shell (§I.6). The canonical fiber's compact part is therefore the spin phase, and the theory may legitimately constrain: spin structures, phase holonomy, chirality, principal spinors, allowed connections, topological charge, geometric relations among mass, charge and rotation, and the availability of zero modes.

## VII.2 What it does not [T]

$$\text{spinorial shell geometry}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{fermionic anticommutation}$$

Newman–Penrose spinors are **classical, commuting** geometric spinors. Grassmann-odd quantum fields are a further structure, and the implication is blocked by type, not by difficulty: Grassmann-odd variables anticommute, and after quantization fermionic creation operators obey anticommutation relations, so that $(a^\dagger)^2 = 0$ — the exclusion principle. Nothing in a spin bundle produces that. **Any such derivation remains open.**

## VII.3 Statistics and exclusion are inputs, unchanged [T]

Spin–statistics, anticommutation and the Pauli exclusion principle enter this theory **exactly as they enter ordinary quantum field theory**, and nothing in v15 modifies, derives or threatens them.

*A note on what is not claimed.* Earlier drafts invoked the Finkelstein–Rubinstein argument — that exchanging two identical particles is locally homotopic to rotating one by $2\pi$ — to say statistics proceed as usual. **That invocation is withdrawn** (§XI.1). FR is a statement about loops in the configuration space of extended topological solitons, and the exchange/rotation identification depends on that configuration space's topology; it is not a theorem that a spacetime spin bundle by itself delivers fermionic statistics. Unless and until actual soliton configuration spaces are constructed here, the safe and sufficient statement is the one above, resting on §VII.2.

## VII.4 Twin parity [O]

The frame bundle of $\mathbb{RP}^3 = SO(3)$ is $SO(3)\times SO(3)$, with $\pi_1 = \mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$: **two independent** generators, a frame rotation (giving spin) and a trip around the twin loop (giving a parity $\tau = \pm1$). It is tempting to read the two $\mathbb{Z}_2$ factors as two independent particle quantum numbers. **That reading is not established, and the section is tagged open for that reason.** $\mathbb{RP}^3$ does have two spin structures, since $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^3;\mathbb{Z}_2) = \mathbb{Z}_2$; but the relation between the base loop, the frame rotation, the *chosen* spin structure, and a genuinely independent label on a field is subtler than reading off two factors of $\pi_1$. Settling it is an associated-bundle representation problem, not a homotopy count, and it has not been worked through here **[O]**.

# PART VIII — STATIC REGRESSION AND TESTS

## VIII.1 The static great-circle realization [S/D]

*An earlier draft claimed to **derive** this from topology. That claim is withdrawn — three steps of it were wrong (§XI.1). What follows is an exact construction of the realization, with its one assumption marked as an assumption.*

The intended specialization is

$$\mathcal{M}_{\rm static}\sim\mathbb{R}_t\times S^4,\qquad B_{\rm rep}^{\rm static}\sim\mathbb{R}_t\times S^3,\qquad B_{\rm grav}^{\rm static}\sim\mathbb{R}_t\times\mathbb{RP}^3$$

**v34.0 note — the pencil as a Law II solution branch, its measure, and the radial trap [S/T].** Under the v34.0 ontology (governing note; Part III) the great-circle pencil below is the intended **dominant-primary solution** of a universal matter-responsive Law II, not an axiom: what is derived here *given* the pencil is the $\mathbb{RP}^3$ quotient and the $S^3$ bisection; what is not derived is the selection of the pencil by matter, any radial behaviour *within* a leaf (at $\theta = \pi/2$ the tangent $\partial_\theta X = -p$ is normal to the leaf, so the pencil realizes extrinsic radial passage through $S^4$, and an intrinsic radial readout on the leaf is a separate map), the pole dynamics, and generic quotient regularity. Two exact facts about this pencil are established in §XXIX.9 and retyped in §XXIX.10 (v34.1, R56–R58): on the regular stratum the volume form of $S^4(\ell)$ disintegrates along the meridian arcs with density $\ell|\sin\theta|^3d\theta$ relative to the round $\mathbb{RP}^3$ measure, which conserves the total of every *integrable* density exactly ($M_{\rm grav} = M_{\mathcal M}$, no doubling, no pole overcounting for smooth densities), reduces matter on the equatorial leaf with weight $\sin^3(\pi/2) = 1$ — the retired two-crossing rule as a special case — and reduces any *smooth* distribution axisymmetric about the poles to a **uniform** base source; a point mass *at* the pole has no canonical reduction (its uniform image is an isotropic-core prescription, §XXIX.10). The parameter space of the circles is $\mathbb{RP}^3$, but the circles share the poles and are not disjoint fibers of a map on $S^4$: "complete fibers" here means the regular $\mathbb{RP}^3$ reduction — connected leaves indexed by $S^3$ plus the pairing $n\sim-n$, two open arcs per fiber — and a genuine fibration exists only on a resolved space. The kinematic alignment control of §XXIX.9 reproduces the pencil's *regular directions* as the line field $[\nabla V]$ of a pole-concentrated source, by symmetry — an unoriented gradient field gives open arcs terminating at the poles, not closed fibers; the pairing and the core completion are additional data — while for two comparable sources it produces two basins with a separatrix.

with dimensions $1+4 = 5$, $1+3 = 4$, $1+3 = 4$ **[V]**.

### The assumption [S]

> **In the static limit, the meridian structure is the antipodal great-circle pencil.** It is a *pencil*, not a foliation: distinct meridians meet at the two poles, which form a common singular set. Nothing in Law 0 or in the topology of $S^4$ forces this, and it is adopted as a structural choice.

### The construction, and the quotient [D/V]

Embed $S^4\subset\mathbb{R}^5$ and fix an axis $p\in S^4$, with poles $\pm p$. For each unit vector $n$ in the 3-sphere of $p^\perp$, form the **2-plane**

$$P_n = \operatorname{span}(p,n),\qquad C_n = P_n\cap S^4$$

Then $C_n$ is a great circle through both poles — verified: every point $\cos t\,p+\sin t\,n$ has unit norm, and $t = 0,\pi$ give $\pm p$ **[V]**. And since a plane is unchanged by negating a spanning vector,

$$P_n = P_{-n}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_n = C_{-n}$$

verified pointwise **[V]**. So the meridians are in bijection with $S^3$ modulo the antipodal map:

$$\boxed{\ \text{space of meridians} = S^3/\{\pm1\} = \mathbb{RP}^3\ }$$

**exactly**, with no index theory, no foliation language, and no claim about closed orbits. And the bisection follows immediately: $C_n$ meets the equatorial $S^3$ at $n$ and at $-n$, the two points of §II.3.

### What is derived, and what is not

$$\text{antipodal great-circle pencil}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb{RP}^3\qquad\textbf{[D]}$$
$$\text{Law 0} + \text{topology}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{antipodal great-circle pencil}\qquad\textbf{[O]}$$

The first is exact. The second is **not available**, and the attempt to supply it is retired (§XI.1).

**The remaining regression, in order [O]:** derive the quotient metric and its Green's function on $\mathbb{RP}^3$; recover the geodesic and orbit equations; **then** reassert the numbers of §IV.8.

## VIII.2 The golf ball [D]

*The question was: does a small body get a Hopf structure of its own, or does a large nearby body dominate?*

**In this version the question has a clean answer, and a different one from before.** The fiber is supplied by spin geometry, and every shell about every worldline carries a unit class:

$$|c_1| = 1$$

independent of the body's mass, its neighbours, or any parameter, with the sign induced globally by orientation and restriction rather than chosen per shell (Structure III). **A golf ball's shells carry the same unit class as Earth's.** There is no competition, no crossover radius, no dependence on what else is nearby — because the structure is a fact about the rotation group acting on a shell, not a tally of matter.

> Earlier versions answered this with a mass-proportional winding number, $M/m_{\rm unit}$ — $2.7\times10^{25}$ for the ball and $3.6\times10^{51}$ for Earth — together with a "quantization fork" over the value of $m_{\rm unit}$ and a crossover at $0.56\,\mu$m where Earth's flux overtook the ball's. **All of that is retired** (§XI.1). It presupposed a posited circle whose class matter was free to set; here the circle is derived and its class is fixed.

**What remains testable is nothing, here.** The class is the same everywhere, so it distinguishes no two situations, and Maxwell's pullback is $U(1)_H$-invariant in any case.

## VIII.3 The Machian direction [T/D/V]

**v34.0 note.** The unit Hopf class $|c_1| = 1$ of this section is source-independent and topological; it is to be kept distinct from the matter-responsive meridian *orientation and foliation* that Law II (v34.0 restatement, Part III) is to select. A stronger primary may dominate the meridian configuration without changing the topological unit charge and without trivially changing $G$; the Machian direction of this section is the selection of orientation by matter, not of the class.

Vacuum general relativity already has the symmetry $(g,M)\to(\lambda^2g,\lambda M)$: every Schwarzschild exterior *is* a rescaled copy of every other, with mass the scale. So "isomorphic shells up to scale" is true and yields nothing new — the scale it fixes is mass, not size, and compactness $r_s/R$ ($1.4\times10^{-9}$ for Earth, $3.2\times10^{-27}$ for a golf ball) is untouched.

Rescaling $r_s$ with $GM$ fixed is **inconsistent**, since $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is one number whenever the exterior has a single source. Separating the horizon from the far-field coupling would require the near field to be sourced by something the far field does not see.

> Earlier versions offered one: the flux energy $|F_\oplus+F_g|^2$ has a cross term present only when Earth is, giving the ball a near field that differs alone and in company, bounded by Mercury at $3\times10^{-4}$. **That is retired with the flux sector** (§XI.1). **So the Machian proposal now has no realizable form in the theory at all** — which is the honest position, and worth stating rather than leaving a retired mechanism standing in for one.

**A local Mach relation fails [V]:** reading $GM/c^2\ell = \pi/2$ with $\ell$ a sphere of influence gives $5\times10^{11}G$ for Earth and $3\times10^{22}G$ for the golf ball. The Mach relation closes a *universe*.

**Emergent $G$ [O]:** an open coupling problem, not a theorem. ADM and Komar masses carry $G$ in the conventional normalization, but matter Lagrangians contain inertial and rest-mass parameters that require no solution of Einstein's equations. The real difficulty is to define an operationally appropriate mass variable and show that a candidate emergent coupling reproduces **both** the inertial and the gravitational roles. *An earlier categorical claim — that $G$ is emergent iff mass has a $G$-free definition, and general relativity has none — is too strong and is retired* (§XI.1).

**The central mass and the rendering branch (version 27) [T/S].** Part XXII's landing raised the question again from the matter side: could the huge central mass that privileges the meridians also fix the gravitational readout, even the value of $G$? It cannot fix $G$: in the frozen two-crossing model $G$ and $\ell$ remain its free constants, and Law I reads $G_{\mu\nu}[g_G]+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi GT^{(g)}_{\mu\nu}$ with $G$ a universal coupling input. What the primary source determines is the realized gravitational geometry, $T^{(g)}\to g_G$, and hence the locked fiber-length profile; and, if Part XXII's branch survives, it also determines the *rendering* — a matter–history selection operator $K_{\rm sel}[T,\Xi,\nabla^\pm]$ on the two-mode space selecting the electron-accessible branch $P_\ell$, after which the projector algebra enforces exact neutrino neutrality (§XXII.13). So the accurate unification available now is that *one matter and history configuration controls both which gravitational geometry is realized and which electromagnetic rendering is realized*, $T^{(g)}\to g_G\to$ fiber geometry alongside $K_{\rm sel}\to P_\ell\to Q_\nu = 0$, while $G$ itself stays a universal coefficient. The only legitimate route from there to the value of $G$ is the one this section already names in a new form: a parent action $S_{\rm parent} = S_{\rm geom}+S_{\rm mode}+S_{\rm matter}$ in which the Einstein coefficient $1/16\pi G$ and the stiffness of the mode-selector sector descend from one canonical normalization — which would have to meet the same test as any emergent coupling here, reproducing both the inertial and the gravitational roles of mass. Neither branch is there.

## VIII.4 The required constructions [O]

1. Construct an explicit $E$ whose shell restrictions are the stated $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ lifts, over $\mathcal{M}$ minus the secondary meridians (§II.1), with a smooth five-dimensional quotient away from controlled singular loci.
2. Show the complex bundle's reduction to $U(1)\to SU(2)\to S^2$ on the Lorentzian slice, covariantly.
3. Define the complex normal bundle and shell lift along a general non-null complex worldline.
4. Carry the shell lift consistently through Schwarzschild $\to$ Kerr.
5. **Derive** $L_H = \Omega L_H^{\rm ref}$ rather than impose it.
6. Determine whether the two open connection components have any role at all, from the action rather than by assignment.
7. Derive the meridian structure from canonical data.
8. Recover $S^4\to\mathbb{RP}^3$ and the barren twin.
9. Re-derive the $v^2$ family in the recovered static sector.
10. Compute what stress-energy an observer infers by applying Einstein's equation on $B_{\rm rep}$ instead of $B_{\rm grav}$ — **the dark-sector target**, and the calculation that would make the architecture phenomenological.
11. Verify the twin stays optically barren.
12. Keep the spin-statistics firewall: do not identify the geometric spin lift with Grassmann parity.

# PART IX — THE ACTION TARGET [O]

A successful action should make both information reductions automatic:

$$S = S_{\rm EH}[B_{\rm grav},g_G] + S_{\rm matter}[B_{\rm rep},\psi,A] + S_{\rm can}\big[E,\hat g,\mathcal{A}_H^{\circ},\widehat{\mathcal{U} }_{\rm mer},\rho_E\big]$$

Here $\mathcal A_H^{\circ}$ is the principal connection on the regular stratum: a principal connection satisfies $\mathcal A_H(X_H) = 1$, which cannot hold where the generator vanishes (§II.2). Variation with respect to $g_G$ should produce the meridian-reduced source; constraints on the canonical metric should produce the fiber-length locking; and if the canonical connection's two open components are to acquire a role, it must come from there rather than from an assignment made by hand. **Until such an action exists, the split is architectural rather than final.**

## IX.1 The canonical metric in bundle form — the parsimonious target [T/V/D/O]

*Parts 0–IX are frozen; this section adds a target to Part IX, not a law. It adopts the one ansatz for $\hat g$ that packages the frozen blocks into a single object, derives what follows, and tests the first candidate condition.*

**The ansatz [D].** On the regular stratum $E^\circ$, take the canonical metric in bundle form,

$$\hat g = \pi_H^*g_{\mathcal M} + R_H^2\,\vartheta^2,\qquad \vartheta = d\chi+\mathcal A_H,\qquad R_H = \frac{L_H}{2\pi}$$

the standard adapted metric of a circle bundle. It contains exactly the frozen $3+1+2$ blocks of §III.3 — the base metric, the fiber length, the connection's cross-components — and nothing else. Structure III supplies $\mathcal A_H$ with its unit class on linking spheres; Law I supplies $L_H$ through the locking; the base metric is the middle space's. So $\hat g$ carries no new freedom. What it lacks is the condition that selects it.

**Berry's phase, with a size [T].** Lifting a loop $\gamma$ of the middle space horizontally returns the fiber rotated by

$$\Delta\chi = \oint_\gamma\mathcal A_H = \int_\Sigma F_H\pmod{2\pi}$$

— for the canonical Hopf connection, half the solid angle the loop encloses on its shell; a full shell gives $2\pi$, the unit class. The theory adds what the Bloch-sphere treatment lacks. The fiber has a length, so the rotation is a displacement,

$$\Delta s_H = \frac{L_H}{2\pi}\,\Delta\chi$$

**$F_H$ says how far around the fiber a loop carries you; $L_H$ says how far that is.** Two identical loops at different potentials acquire the same angle and different displacements. The connection curvature of Part XIII's optical sector is the same mechanism — curvature as the failure of horizontal lifts to close — on a different connection; for a deformed connection at fixed class it is the curvature flux, not the enclosed area, that rotates the fiber, and a non-contractible loop can carry holonomy with no curvature at all, the distinction §XIII.9 rests on.

**What the ansatz gives for free [T].** By O'Neill's formulas the curvature of $\hat g$ separates into the base curvature, a term in $R_H^2|F_H|^2$, and terms in the gradient and Laplacian of $R_H$ — schematically $\hat R = R_{\mathcal M}-\tfrac14R_H^2|F_H|^2-2R_H^{-1}\Delta R_H$. Read from the base's side, this is the only place where fiber length and twisting *could* feed curvature downstairs, and the Berger spheres show the catch: stretching $S^3$ along its Hopf fibers changes the curvature of $S^3$ and leaves the quotient $S^2$ untouched. Fiber length reaches the quotient only through a condition on $\hat g$. The action target of this part therefore becomes one question:

> **Given $\hat g$ in bundle form, what condition on $\hat g$ makes the quotient obey Law I?**

**The first candidate fails [V].** The simplest condition — Einstein's vacuum equations on $E$ — turns the ansatz into ordinary Kaluza–Klein theory, in which every source's unit Hopf class is a Kaluza–Klein monopole. That is checkable, and the check is decisive:

| configuration, unit class on every sphere | fiber toward the source | Ricci-flat |
|:--|:--|:--|
| the Kaluza–Klein monopole (Euclidean Taub–NUT), $R_H = 4m\,(1+2m/r)^{-1/2}$ | shrinks, $1-m/r$ | **yes** — the code's validation |
| Law I's locking on isotropic Schwarzschild, $R_H = R_0\,(1+GM/2r)^2$ | grows, $1+GM/r$ | **no** — $\hat R_{\chi\chi}$ and $\hat R_{tt}$ both nonzero |

The failure is qualitative: the vacuum fiber shrinks toward a source where the locking's grows — Obstruction 1 of §XI.3 once more, now as a sign. And the condition would make the fiber's absolute size observable: the monopole's stress on the base is proportional to $R_H^2/r^4$, which with the document's normalization $L_H^{\rm ref} = 2\pi\ell$ exceeds the Sun's gravity at 1 AU by $5\times10^{26}$, and with a Planck-scale fiber falls to $10^{-85}$. **Einstein–Hilbert on $E$ is not the canonical action.**

**The fork this leaves [D/O].** Either the locking's sign is right, and the condition on $\hat g$ is something other than vacuum Einstein — the collapse core of §II.2 is then *not* Taub–NUT, since the fiber must grow before it collapses; or the unique smooth Ricci-flat completion is right, the fiber shrinks toward sources, and the spin-phase argument behind the locking (§I.6, §III.2) has to be re-examined. The convention $L_H^{\rm ref} = 2\pi\ell$ is untested on either branch: nothing in Parts 0–IX measures the fiber's absolute size, and the condition on $\hat g$ is what would.
