## XXVIII.13 The angular complex shell as a Grauert tube: continued Berry transport and the mathematical precursor of Part XV's Weyl pair [T/V/D/O]

**The complexified base, from real geometry [T/V].** Part XV.7 needs a complexified base with its complex structure $J_{\rm base}$ and imaginary directions $dy^j$, and Part I.2 asserts the complex shell to be the affine quadric $Q^2_{\rm aff} = \{z\in\mathbb C^3: z\cdot z = 1\}$. A theorem of complex geometry supplies both from the real axis sphere alone. For a real-analytic Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ there is, on a tube $\{|v|<r\}$ in $TM$, a unique complex structure *adapted* to $g$ — the Grauert tube of Guillemin–Stenzel and Lempert–Szőke (1991), characterized by the condition that for every geodesic $\gamma$ the strip map $\sigma+i\tau\mapsto\tau\gamma'(\sigma)$ is holomorphic; it exists iff $g$ is real-analytic and is unique when it exists. For the round $S^2$ the tube is entire and $(TS^2,J_{\rm adapted})$ is biholomorphic to the quadric $\{z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2 = 1\}$. The map is explicit, $\Phi(x,v) = \cosh|v|\,x+i\,\sinh|v|\,v/|v|$, and was checked: $\Phi\cdot\Phi = 1$ to $10^{-14}$; for the geodesic $\gamma(s) = \cos s\,x+\sin s\,v$ the strip $\Phi(\gamma(s),t\gamma'(s)) = \cos(s+it)\,x+\sin(s+it)\,v$ is holomorphic in $s+it$ (Cauchy–Riemann residual $5\times10^{-11}$), which is the adapted condition, so by uniqueness $\Phi$ carries *the* adapted structure; and at the zero section $d\Phi(w^h) = w$, $d\Phi(w^v) = iw$, so $J_{\rm base}$ swaps the horizontal and vertical lifts: *the imaginary-normal direction at a real history point is the real tangent fiber of the axis sphere*, and the complexified coordinates $(\zeta,w) = (\theta+i\eta,\ \phi+i\chi)$ are holomorphic coordinates on the quadric with $J\partial_\theta = \partial_\eta$, $J\partial_\phi = \partial_\chi$. So Part I.2's complex shell is the unique adapted complexification of the real axis sphere: the quadric is reconstructed from the real rest space and its round metric with no complex coordinate inserted, and the "imaginary directions" $dy^j$ of Part XV.7 are, in the angular sector, nothing but tangent vectors to the real sphere. The real structure of the tube is the fiber antipodal map $v\mapsto-v$, which is complex conjugation on the quadric ($\overline{\Phi(x,v)} = \Phi(x,-v)$, checked), fixing the real sphere.

**The unique holomorphic extension, and XV.7's structure derived [T/V].** The spin-lift connection of §XXVIII.12 is real-analytic, so by the identity theorem it has a unique holomorphic extension to the tube; in ambient coordinates it is
$$\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = i\,\frac{z_1\,dz_2-z_2\,dz_1}{2(1+z_3)},$$
a complex-linear one-form on $TQ$. Checked: on the real sphere $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}(\partial_\phi) = i\beta_N$ and $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}(\partial_\theta) = 0$; it is of type $(1,0)$, $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}(J_{\rm base}W) = i\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}(W)$; and in the holomorphic coordinates $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = i\,b(\zeta)\,dw$ with $b(\zeta) = \tfrac12(1-\cos\zeta)$ the analytic continuation of $b(\theta)$ — exactly XV.7's $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = i\,b_j(z)\,dz^j$ with $b_j$ real on the real locus. Three of XV.7's consequences follow as the Cauchy–Riemann equations of the extension, each checked: the firewall $A|_{TE} = {\rm Re}\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}|_{\rm real\ directions} = 0$; $A(J_{\rm base}w) = -\mathcal A_H(w)$ for real $w$ ($-0.151647$ against $-0.151647$); and the mixed-curvature identity, $F_A(\partial_\theta,J\partial_\phi) = -F_H(\partial_\theta,\partial_\phi)$ and $F_A(\partial_\phi,J\partial_\theta) = -F_H(\partial_\phi,\partial_\theta)$ with $F_H = \tfrac12\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, while $F_A$ vanishes on real–real and imaginary–imaginary pairs at the real locus — *purely mixed*. The identity $F_A(v,J_{\rm base}w) = -F_H(v,w)$ is therefore not an independent datum to be inserted or tested: it is the statement that $F_{\mathbb C} = d\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ is a holomorphic $(2,0)$-form, forced by holomorphy. The relationship between $J_{\rm base}$ and the fiber's $i$, which the referee required to be explained rather than identified by notation, is the type-$(1,0)$ condition $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}\circ J_{\rm base} = i\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ — they act on different spaces ($TQ$ and the fiber of $L_H$) and are related by the holomorphy of the connection, which the identity theorem forces. Part I.3's complex Hopf lift $\mathbb C^\times\to SL(2,\mathbb C)\to Q^2_{\rm aff}$ is the same object, stated exactly: with $c = \cos\tfrac\zeta2$, $s = \sin\tfrac\zeta2$, the matrix $g(\zeta,w) = \begin{psmallmatrix}c&-e^{-iw}s\\ e^{iw}s&c\end{psmallmatrix}$ has $\det g = c^2+s^2 = 1$, its first column is the extended spinor $\psi = (c,\ e^{iw}s)$, the first row of $g^{-1}$ is $\tilde\psi^T = (c,\ e^{-iw}s)$ with $\tilde\psi^T\psi = 1$, and the $(1,1)$ component of its Maurer–Cartan form is the connection, $(g^{-1}dg)_{11} = \tilde\psi^T d\psi = \mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ (checked off the real locus to $10^{-6}$ — v32.19 wrote $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}/i$, a transcription error, the computation having given equality): the complex Hopf lift is an explicit $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ frame over the quadric, and the extended connection is one component of its Maurer–Cartan form, the holomorphic extension of the real spin frame bundle. The displayed $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ is the northern-chart form, singular where $1+z_3 = 0$ on the complexified southern locus; the southern form is $\mathcal A^S_{\mathbb C} = -i(z_1dz_2-z_2dz_1)/(2(1-z_3))$, and on the overlap $\mathcal A^N_{\mathbb C}-\mathcal A^S_{\mathbb C} = i\,dw$ (checked): the transition is the complexified unit-winding $e^{iw} = e^{i\phi}e^{-\chi}$, a $\mathbb C^\times$-valued function of modulus $e^{-\chi}$, unimodular on the real locus, so the nontrivial Hopf topology survives complexification as a holomorphic $\mathbb C^\times$-bundle of degree one, described by local holomorphic forms and this transition exactly as the real Hopf connection is. The curvature is global: $F_{\mathbb C} = d\mathcal A^N_{\mathbb C} = d\mathcal A^S_{\mathbb C} = \tfrac i2\,z\cdot(dz\times dz)/2 = \tfrac i2\Omega_{\rm hol}$ with $\Omega_{\rm hol}$ the holomorphic volume form of the quadric (checked), so the scale part of a closed-loop holonomy is gauge-invariant.

**The exchange, the Weyl pair, and the scale holonomy as the continued Berry phase [T/V].** XV.7's exchange $\rho_E$ with equivariance $\rho_E^*\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = -\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} }$ is derived: complex conjugation on the quadric — the tube's real structure $v\mapsto-v$ — satisfies $c^*\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = -\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} }$ exactly (checked), so a *conjugate history* is a history with reversed fiber displacement, and $\int_{\bar\gamma}\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = -\overline{\int_\gamma\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} }$: the scale (real part) reverses and the phase (imaginary part) is fixed — on the $\mathbb C^\times$ holonomy this is $w\mapsto1/\bar w$, which is XV.7's $\rho_E$ and the split involution $\rho$ of §XXVIII.11, now derived rather than identified. The structure is explicit at the level of holonomies. Along a latitude loop at colatitude $\theta_0$ with a transverse (meridional) fiber displacement $\tau$, the lifted loop sits at complex colatitude $\zeta = \theta_0+i\tau$, and $\oint\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = i\,\Phi(\theta_0+i\tau)$ with $\Phi(\theta) = \pi(1-\cos\theta) = \Omega/2$ the real Berry phase: the $\mathbb C^\times$ holonomy is $e^{\eta+i\varphi}$ with
$$\eta = -{\rm Im}\,\Phi(\theta_0+i\tau) = -\pi\sin\theta_0\sinh\tau,\qquad \varphi = {\rm Re}\,\Phi(\theta_0+i\tau) = \pi(1-\cos\theta_0\cosh\tau)$$
(checked by direct line integration on the quadric: $-0.61631+0.62983i$ at $\theta_0 = 0.7$, $\tau = 0.3$, against the formula; $\tau\to-\tau$ reverses $\eta$ and fixes $\varphi$; $\tau = 0$ gives $\eta = 0$, $\varphi = \Omega/2$). *The scale holonomy of a complex history is minus the imaginary part of the analytically continued phase holonomy, and its phase is the real part.* The Weyl one-form along the displaced history is $A_\gamma = -\tfrac12\sin\theta_0\sinh\tau\,d\phi$ (checked), $+\tfrac12\sin\theta_0\sinh\tau\,d\phi$ along its conjugate, with mean zero — an exchange-related pair of scalar scale transports with Levi-Civita as the mean. The claim is stated at its exact strength, in the referee's words: *the continued angular Berry connection realizes the phase–scale algebra, the real-locus firewall, and the exchange-odd scalar holonomy anticipated by Part XV; it supplies a mathematically explicit precursor of the Weyl pair; identifying this precursor with the two affine Weyl connections $\nabla^\pm$ on the physical middle space requires an independently constructed descent and a comparison of parallel transports.* Part XV's $\nabla^\pm$ are affine connections on the middle-space tangent bundle, $\Gamma^{\pm a}{}_{bc} = \Gamma^a{}_{bc}\pm(\delta^a_bA_c+\delta^a_cA_b-h_{bc}A^a)$, and to derive them as physical connections one needs a real one-form $A$ on the middle-space base, a geometrically specified map from the complexified angular-history bundle to that base, a demonstration that the resulting connections transform and descend consistently, and the relation between their affine transport and the scalar $\mathbb C^\times$ holonomy; their common null-geodesic property and Levi-Civita mean follow algebraically once a Weyl one-form is supplied, so the definition of the Weyl connections is not a derivation of their physical origin, and the missing work is why the physical geometry supplies this particular one-form. Two features of the holonomy are recorded because they bound the physics. A *longitudinal* fiber displacement, along the loop's own velocity, gives *no* scale holonomy (checked, $4\times10^{-14}$) — the lifted loop then sits at real colatitude with constant imaginary azimuth, where $b$ is real — so scale arises only from displacement transverse to the history, in the direction along which the phase potential varies; and to first order $\eta\simeq-\tau\,d\Phi/d\theta$, the displacement times the gradient of the phase holonomy across the loop, which is Cauchy–Riemann at the level of holonomies.

**Metricity: the firewall twice [T].** For a connection $\mathbb B = \alpha I+\beta\mathbb J$ on a real rank-two metric bundle, metric compatibility is skew-adjointness of the connection matrix, and $\mathbb B^T+\mathbb B = 2\alpha I$ (checked), so $\nabla g_E = 0\Rightarrow\alpha = 0$: a metric-compatible spin connection has no real scale component, and its real transport is purely rotational, $\mathbb B_{\rm real} = \beta\mathbb J$. The spin lift of Levi-Civita is metric-compatible, so the firewall $A|_{TE} = 0$ holds for it by metricity, independently of the holomorphic derivation above — and the two agree. This is a positive result and a restriction at once: it supplies XV.7's firewall automatically for the reconstructed connection, and it means that no reinterpretation of ordinary real holonomy can produce a scale response; scale requires the fiber displacement, which is the additional operation Part XV's analytic continuation was always supplying. It does not prove that the *physical* middle-space Weyl one-form vanishes on the real locus, which needs the physical connection identified with this one.

**What is derived, and what is not [D/O].** Derived, for the angular sector and from the real axis sphere with its round metric: the complex shell of Part I.2 as the Grauert tube; the complex Hopf lift of Part I.3 as the holomorphic extension of the real spin frame bundle; XV.7's $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = i\,b_j(z)dz^j$, its firewall, $A(Jw) = -\mathcal A_H(w)$, the mixed-curvature identity, the exchange $\rho_E$ and its equivariance; the scalar precursor of XV.1's pair, an exchange-related pair of scale transports with Levi-Civita as the mean; and the scale holonomy in closed form as the continued Berry phase. Not derived: *the physical selection of the fiber displacement.* Real histories carry no scale (twice over), and a complex history's scale is set by its transverse fiber displacement $\tau$, a tangent vector to the axis sphere; which admissible histories carry such a displacement, and what fixes its magnitude, is the physics Part XXVII's history classes must supply — a transverse displacement of a history is a tangent vector field along it, the shape of a Jacobi field, so the identification of Part XXVII's imaginary-normal direction with the fiber displacement is the natural conjecture and is open. *The non-angular sector.* The Grauert-tube theorem is Riemannian; it complexifies the real rest-space geometry and the axis sphere, not the middle space with its conformal null structure $[h]$, on which no adapted complex structure is available by this theorem — so XV.1's descent to the middle-space $\nabla^\pm$ stays conditional, with its obstruction now named: the step from a Riemannian rest-space sector to a conformal-null base. The shell components beyond the angular Hopf curvature (§XXVI.11) are not constructed. *The readout.* $\eta$ is a geometric holonomy of a complex history; its relation to a frequency ratio $1+z = e^\eta$ needs the complex relative transport of Part XXVII's open problem 1 and is not claimed. *The circularity.* The real rest space and its round metric are taken as real primitives, so this is a reconstruction of Parts I.2–I.3 and XV.7 from real data already in the theory, not a derivation of all primitive complex canonical geometry from independently established centrade structure, which remains the larger objective. The reconstruction ledger is amended accordingly, and the tally becomes: the algebra yes; the Hopf topology and connection yes; the complex shell and the holomorphic scalar precursor of the bi-connection, for the angular sector, yes, with the scale a derived function of a fiber displacement; the pair reading of Part XXVII's histories supplying that displacement as a canonical candidate with a definite, bounded scale (§XXVIII.14); the affine Weyl pair on the conformal-null middle space and the readout not.

## XXVIII.14 The pair as a complex history: the first-variation law, the canonical map from a history variation into the Grauert tube, and the round and Berger benchmarks [T/V/D/O]

**The first-variation law, with its sign [T/V].** The referee's observation is exact and was checked: for a real loop $\gamma$ on the axis sphere with tangent $k$ and an imaginary displacement $Y$ — a tangent field along $\gamma$, lifted into the tube as $\Phi(\gamma,\epsilon Y)$ — the continued holonomy changes at first order by
$$\Delta{\rm Re}\log{\rm Hol} = -\epsilon\int_\gamma F_H(Y,k)\,ds+O(\epsilon^3),\qquad \Delta{\rm Im}\log{\rm Hol} = O(\epsilon^2),$$
the scale odd in the displacement with a cubic correction and the phase even with a quadratic one (a real displacement gives $+i\epsilon\int F_H(Y,k)\,ds$ at first order, a pure phase), because $F_{\mathbb C}(iY,k) = i\cdot iF_H(Y,k)$; the constant is $\mathcal C = -1$ in the convention ${\rm Hol} = \exp\oint\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$, $F_H = \tfrac12\,x\cdot(V\times W)$ (checked on a random loop with a random transverse field: ratio $0.9998$ at $\epsilon = 0.05$, the phase change $O(\epsilon^2)$). The holonomy is computed gauge-invariantly as the flux of the global $F_{\mathbb C} = \tfrac i2\Omega_{\rm hol}$ through the surface swept by the displacement, which avoids the chart issue of §XXVIII.13.

**A natural candidate map from a pair of histories to a complex history [T/V].** Part XXVII's objects are pairs of admissible histories $(\gamma_+,\gamma_-)$ on the arena with common endpoints and a separation between them. The construction that sends such a pair into the tube is the following; every step is natural and no parameter is chosen, but — as the audit below shows — the geometry does not uniquely force it, and it is a candidate assignment rather than the canonical physical identification. Project both members to the axis sphere by the Hopf fibration the arena carries, $\pi(q) = q\mathbf e_3q^{-1}$ — the fibration the Berger squashing preserves; take the real history to be the normalized mean of the projections, $x(s)$, and the imaginary displacement to be the tangential half-separation, $v(s) = \tfrac12\,P_{x}\big(\pi\gamma_+(s)-\pi\gamma_-(s)\big)$; the complex history is $\Phi(x(s),v(s))$, with real endpoints since the members share theirs. Its properties: it is equivariant under the arena's symmetry, since $\pi$ and every operation are; the exchange of the two members sends $v\to-v$, so *exchanging the pair is the conjugation $\rho_E$* — the exchange-odd scalar holonomy of §XXVIII.13 is the exchange of Part XXVII's pair; and it is independent of the correspondence between the members at first order, because a longitudinal displacement contributes $F_H(k,k) = 0$ (checked: the equal-fraction and the arc-length-matched correspondences agree to five digits), so the leading-order scale is a correspondence-independent invariant of the pair. The leading-order law follows from the first variation: with $J = 2v$ the separation,
$$\eta = -\tfrac12\int F_H(J,k)\,ds+O(J^3) = -\tfrac12\,\Phi_{\rm lune} = -\tfrac14\,\Omega_{\rm lune},$$
*minus half the real Hopf flux through the lune between the projected members*, i.e. minus a quarter of the solid angle the pair's projections enclose on the axis sphere — the complex history's scale is set by the real relative Berry phase of the pair, which is the real sector's own invariant. This is the referee's $\eta_\Xi = \mathcal C\int F_H(Y_\Xi,k_\Xi)\,ds$ with $Y_\Xi$ the projected half-separation and $\mathcal C = -1$, neither tuned — and, as the audit shows, with $F_H$ the curvature of a *selected* fibration, so that $\eta$ is an invariant of the pair together with the fibration.

**The round-arena benchmark [T/V].** On the round arena the pair is two geodesics from the source to its antipode, where all geodesics focus — the configuration whose real $SO(3)$ loop holonomy §XXVII.9 found to be the identity. With initial directions $\mathbf u_\pm = \cos\tfrac\delta2\,\mathbf u\pm\sin\tfrac\delta2\,\mathbf e$, the scale is
$$\eta = \pi\,\sin\tfrac\delta2\;\times\;(\text{fiber component of }\mathbf e),$$
checked against the surface integral ($0.15718$ against $\pi\sin0.05 = 0.15701$; $0.47379$ against $0.46947$ at $\delta = 0.3$, the difference the $O(\delta^3)$ term) with $\eta/\Phi_{\rm lune} = -0.5005$; it vanishes for a horizontal separation and for a mean along the fiber, and the phase vanishes throughout. So the complex reading supplies, for the round antipodal pair, exactly what the real sector could not: a scale, determined by the pair's separation along the Hopf fiber.

**The Berger benchmark: the fold pair across the fold family [V].** The perturbed arena is the Berger arena, and the construction survives it. Reading the fold pair of §§XXVII.1–2 as one complex history gives $\eta = +0.876$, $+0.400$, $+0.181$, $+0.116$ at $\lambda = 0.790$, $0.800$, $0.802$, $0.8023$, openings $32.88^\circ$, $14.98^\circ$, $6.77^\circ$, $4.35^\circ$ — linear in the opening (log–log slope $0.998$, $\eta\simeq1.53\times{\rm opening\ in\ radians}$), vanishing at the fold like the real holonomy of §XXVII.9, with $\eta/\Phi_{\rm lune} = -0.513$, $-0.503$, $-0.501$, $-0.500$ converging on the leading-order law, the phase of the complex-against-mean loop $O({\rm separation}^2)$ and negligible, and the two correspondences agreeing to five digits. At $\lambda = 0.800$ the fold pair's scale is $|\eta| = 0.400$, i.e. $e^{\pm\eta} = 1.49$ or $0.67$: a definite number for the "complex relative transport $\eta$" that §XXVII.9 left to Part XV's extension, derived from the pair's own geometry with nothing inserted.

**The bound, as first stated — withdrawn [R].** v32.20 argued from $|\Phi_{\rm lune}|\le2\pi$ to a universal $|\eta|\le\pi$ and from there to the exclusion of $z_* = 1090$; the audit below shows the inference fails at finite displacement, and both the bound and the exclusion are withdrawn (R11), with what survives stated there.

**Audit of the pair reading (v32.21): domain, uniqueness, admissibility, fibration dependence, and the withdrawn bound [T/V/O].** *The phase term.* The first paragraph's $O(\epsilon^3)$ was correct for the scale and wrong for the complete logarithm: the exact latitude expansion gives $L(\epsilon)-L(0) = -\pi\sin\theta\,\epsilon-\tfrac{i\pi}2\cos\theta\,\epsilon^2+O(\epsilon^3)$ (checked: $-0.202724-0.012024i$ at $\theta = 0.7$, $\epsilon = 0.1$, against $-0.202387$ and $-0.012014i$), so $\Delta{\rm Re}\,L = -\epsilon\int F_H(Y,k)\,ds+O(\epsilon^3)$ and $\Delta{\rm Im}\,L = O(\epsilon^2)$ — the scale odd with a cubic correction, the phase even with a quadratic one, the structural separation the Berger phases of order separation$^2$ already showed. *Domain.* The midpoint is undefined where the projections are antipodal, so the map lives on $\mathcal D = \{(n_+,n_-): n_+\neq-n_-\}$; every pair used was checked to lie inside it, the minimum of $n_+\cdot n_-$ along the path being $+0.615$, $+0.915$, $+0.982$, $+0.993$ for the Berger family and $+0.825$ for the round pair at $\delta = 0.3$ (the round pair at $\delta = 1.5$ reaches $-0.990$ and is near the boundary, which is why its two conventions diverge below). *Uniqueness.* The chordal half-separation $v_{\rm chord} = \sin\tfrac\alpha2\,u$ and the logarithmic $v_{\log} = \tfrac\alpha2\,u$ are both equivariant, exchange-odd and vanish at coincidence, and agree to $O(\alpha^3)$; recomputing the Berger scales with both gives $\eta_{\rm chord}/\eta_{\log} = 0.876/0.901$, $0.4003/0.4025$, $0.1811/0.1813$, $0.11625/0.11631$ — relative differences $2.9\times10^{-2}$, $5.6\times10^{-3}$, $1.1\times10^{-3}$, $4.6\times10^{-4}$, falling as the square of the opening (the absolute discrepancy is cubic, the relative one quadratic; corrected in the next paragraph) — so the fold-family scales are fixed by the history geometry to better than a percent near the fold and the convention matters only at large separation (the round pair at $\delta = 1.5$: $2.45$ against $3.87$). "Canonical" is accordingly replaced by *natural candidate complex-history assignment*: no parameter is chosen, but the geometry does not uniquely force the formula, and a physical history principle must select chordal, logarithmic, or another convention; and a tube curve is not thereby a complex geodesic, an admissible analytic continuation of the null history, or an object transported by the co-middle connection — the tube supplies a place for the displacement, not the history equations. *The admissibility confrontation.* §XXVII.9's criterion for two histories to descend to one common Hopf quotient — commuting relative quaternions — failed for the Berger fold pair at $\lambda = 0.8$ ($\max|[g,g']-1| = 0.098$, axes spread $87^\circ$), and the present construction confirms the same fact in its own terms: the projected members are separated by $23.8^\circ$ at most and $14.3^\circ$ on average along the path, they do not coincide. The midpoint construction is therefore a *different operation* from the common-quotient condition $\pi(\gamma_+) = \pi(\gamma_-)$: it does not solve the old obstruction, it goes around it by manufacturing a third curve from two distinct projected curves, and the requirement has changed — from literal coincidence under one quotient to a relational operation on the pair whose physical meaning must be established independently. That may be what the rendering is; it is recorded as a change of requirement and not as a unification. *Fibration dependence — the decisive test.* The round pair at $\delta = 0.3$ was held fixed and the Hopf axis $\mathbf m$ varied over eight directions: $\eta_{\mathbf m} = +0.474$, $0$, $0$, $+0.391$, $+0.215$, $+0.456$, $+0.261$, $-0.190$, matching $\pi\sin\tfrac\delta2\,(\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m)$ to one percent in every case, with $\mathbf e$ the pair's separation direction in the Lie algebra. The scale is an invariant of *(pair, fibration)*, not of the pair alone — maximal when the fiber axis lies along the separation, zero when orthogonal to it, and reversed when $\mathbf m$ is reversed. A physical selector of $\mathbf m$ is indispensable, and the theorem the branch now needs is the referee's: whether the admissible history constraints force a distinguished $\mathbf m$. On the Berger arena the squashing selects the axis $\mathbf e_3$, which is why its magnitudes are unambiguous; on the round arena, with its $\mathbb{RP}^2$ of fibrations (§XXVII.9), the pair supplies candidate axes but no principle selects among them (next paragraph), and the leading-order law $\eta = \pi\sin\tfrac\delta2\,(\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m)$ exhibits the dependence exactly. *The bound, withdrawn.* The inference $|\eta|\le\pi$ does not follow: $\eta = -\tfrac12\Phi_{\rm lune}$ is a leading-order law, and $|v|\le1$ bounds the argument of $\sinh$, not $\sinh$. The referee's counterexample is confirmed — an equatorial mean with constant meridional displacement $\tau_0 = 0.9$, tapered to zero at the endpoints, gives $|\eta| = 3.056$, $3.157$, $3.191$ as the taper shrinks through $5\%$, $2\%$, $1\%$ of the loop, converging on $\pi\sinh0.9 = 3.225>\pi$ — and a spanning surface may in any case carry multiplicity or winding, so its signed flux is not bounded by one sphere's. What is retained is the leading-order estimate $|\eta|\lesssim\tfrac12|\Phi_{\rm lune}|$ for small separations bounding a simple lune; a bound for all admissible physical pairs would need their actual history constraints, allowable windings and the nonlinear map, and does not exist here. The exclusion of the CMB-scale conjecture is therefore demoted from a result to an open question: the pair reading of one Berger fold pair gives $|\eta|\le0.9$ across the family, far from $7.0$, but nothing proved forbids larger values for other admissible pairs. *Reproduction data.* The Berger velocities, lengths, observer, fibration, correspondence and quadrature are recorded in the toy (`pair_complex_reading`, and the printed table), so the four scales can be recomputed from the trajectories by anyone; until then they are manuscript-reported checks, and $e^{\pm0.400}$ is a transport factor and not a redshift.

**The signed scale is a section of the sign line, and the fibration-selection test (v32.22) [T/V/O].** *The twisted quantity.* The fibration selected by $\mathbf m$ and by $-\mathbf m$ is the same circle foliation with opposite orientation, so the space of unoriented fibrations is $\mathbb{RP}^2$; but $\eta_{-\mathbf m} = -\eta_{\mathbf m}$ — checked *exactly*, not only at leading order ($+0.47379/-0.47379$, $+0.21523/-0.21523$, $+0.45567/-0.45567$ at three axes), since $\pi_{-\mathbf m}$ reverses the orientation of the axis sphere and with it $F_H$. The signed scale is therefore not a function on the space of unoriented fibrations; it is a section $\boldsymbol\eta([\mathbf m]) = \eta_{\mathbf m}\mathbf m\in\Gamma(\gamma^1)$ of the tautological line over $\mathbb{RP}^2$, invariant under $\mathbf m\to-\mathbf m$, locally a number and globally twisted — and at leading order $\boldsymbol\eta = C\,(\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m)\mathbf m = C\,P_{[\mathbf m]}\mathbf e$ with $C = \pi\sin\tfrac\delta2$, the projection of the pair's separation direction onto the fibration line: *the same section as §XXVIII.9's $\boldsymbol\beta_R(\mathbf n) = (\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r)\mathbf n$*, with the pair's separation $\mathbf e$ in the role the background $\mathbf r$ played there. The orientation-bundle mathematics of the attestation toy reappears in a calculation that did not import it: there it governed background-conditioned imaginary orientations, here the history-derived scale as the fibration convention changes. For pairs whose complex-history assignment is defined continuously over every unoriented axis (the domain question is settled for the tested pairs in §XXVIII.15), a nonvanishing global section of the nontrivial $\gamma^1$ is impossible, so the signed-scale section must vanish somewhere; in the leading-order round model its zero locus is the projective equator $\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m = 0$ — the zero-response fibrations required by the same topology that forbade a global imaginary orientation. The correction to the manuscript's language is the referee's: *the unordered fibration determines a splitting magnitude, a line-valued scale datum, and not a signed scale without an additional orientation convention*; only orientation-independent quantities such as $\eta^2$ descend as ordinary scalars. The Berger squashing selects a preferred axis and not an orientation along it, so the fold family's $|\eta|$ is unambiguous once fibration and pair construction are fixed while its sign still needs the ordering the open list already records. *The chordal/logarithmic exponent, corrected.* $v_{\rm chord}-v_{\log} = -\tfrac{\alpha^3}{48}\mathbf u+O(\alpha^5)$ is cubic, but $v_{\log}\sim\tfrac\alpha2\mathbf u$ is first order, so the *relative* discrepancy is $\alpha^2/24$, quadratic; the four reported relative differences fit a log–log slope of $2.04$ against the opening (checked), which is what the mathematics predicts and not the cubic the previous paragraph stated: the absolute discrepancy is cubic in the opening, the relative one quadratic, both vanishing toward the fold (R14). *The pair's own candidate axes.* "Nothing in the pair selects a Hopf axis" was too strong: a round pair of distinct great-circle histories with initial directions $\mathbf u_\pm$ supplies natural unoriented axes — the separation $[\mathbf u_+-\mathbf u_-]$, exchange-symmetric since reversing the difference leaves the projective line fixed and rotation-covariant; the mean $[\mathbf u_++\mathbf u_-]$; and the plane normal $[\mathbf u_+\times\mathbf u_-]$. Evaluated on the fixed round pair they give $\eta = +0.474$, $0$, $0$: the separation axis maximizes $|\eta|$ (it is the maximizer of the leading-order law $C\,\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m$), the other two kill it — three equivariant, exchange-symmetric candidates with three different answers, and choosing the separation axis because it maximizes the scale would be circular if the scale were the thing to derive. The correct statement is the referee's: *the pair supplies natural candidate fibration axes but does not establish which the physical rendering must use.* *The Berger arena makes the problem concrete.* There the squashing distinguishes a fibration the geometry itself singles out — the Berger metric's right-isometry group is $\mathrm{Pin}(2) = U(1)_{\mathbf e_3}\cup\mathbf jU(1)_{\mathbf e_3}$, with the unique invariant axis $[\mathbf e_3]$ unoriented (the theorem of §XXVIII.15) — and it is *not* the pair's separation axis: the two are $60^\circ$ apart along the fold family, with $\eta(\mathbf e_3) = 0.876$ against $\eta_{\rm sep} = 1.202$, $\eta_{\rm mean} = 0.497$, $\eta_{\rm normal} = -0.097$ at $\lambda = 0.79$, and $0.400$ against $0.547$, $0.218$, $-0.051$ at $\lambda = 0.80$. Two distinguished axes, one from the arena's symmetry and one from the pair's geometry, with different scales; no principle in the frozen architecture picks between them, and that choice is the fibration-selection theorem the branch needs — with the arena's own distinguished axis the natural first candidate, since it is the one the frozen rendering (§XXVII.6) already used and the only one that is a property of the arena rather than of the pair. *The selector-independent diagnostic.* Averaging over uniformly distributed axes, $\langle\eta_{\mathbf m}^2\rangle = \tfrac{\pi^2}3\sin^2\tfrac\delta2$ at leading order for the round pair, first computed with sixty random axes as $0.00915$ against $0.00822$ and $0.0831$ against $0.0735$ — an eleven-to-thirteen percent excess that was finite-sample error, resolved by deterministic quadrature in §XXVIII.15 to ratios $1.002$ and $1.018$, the latter the directional law's $O(\delta^2)$ correction; on the Berger family the root-mean-square scale over random axes is $0.711$ and $0.323$ at $\lambda = 0.79$, $0.80$ — a rotation- and sign-invariant number attached to the pair alone, not a substitute for a physical choice of fibration since an average of holonomies is not the transport along one history, but a quantity that separates what belongs to the pair from what belongs to the convention. The research question is thereby restated as the referee restated it — not *do these two paths already project to one history*, which the fold pair answers no, but *does the theory prescribe a relational operation on the two paths whose result is one complex history*, with the chain *physical pair $\to$ physically selected axis and displacement $\to$ complex Berry transport $\to$ middle-space Weyl transport $\to$ observable* having a constructed middle segment and neither end.

**What is open [O].** Five things, in order of weight, the first added by the audit. *Fibration.* The signed scale is a section of the sign line over the $\mathbb{RP}^2$ of fibrations, and its magnitude depends on the axis; the pair supplies candidate axes (separation, mean, plane normal) and the Berger arena supplies its own ($\mathbf e_3$), with different scales, so a derivation $(\gamma_+,\gamma_-)\mapsto[\mathbf m_{\rm phys}]$ from the established history constraints — not by maximizing, minimizing or fitting $\eta$ — is the precondition for the scale to be a property of the pair; $\langle\eta^2\rangle$ is the selector-independent diagnostic meanwhile. *Selection.* The projected half-separation is the canonical candidate for the physical imaginary displacement — equivariant, exchange-odd, correspondence-independent, with the right real-endpoint structure — and not a derivation from the history equations; the referee's requirement stands, that the first arrow in *admissible history variation $\to$ tube displacement $\to$ continued holonomy* be derived independently, and this section supplies the candidate and its properties, not the derivation. *Sign.* $\eta$ is odd under the exchange of the pair, so a redshift $1+z = e^{\pm\eta}$ needs a physical rule ordering the two members, exactly as the observer-side scalar of §XXVII.10 needed one — the exchange $(k_1,k_2,v)\to(k_2,k_1,-v)$ there flips the pseudoscalar, and here flips $\eta$; arrival order is a label where the delays differ and undefined at a tie, so the label-independent datum is $|\eta|$, and the sign is open. *Descent.* The scale is a scalar $\mathbb C^\times$ holonomy on the angular shell; its identification with the affine Weyl pair on the physical middle space is the descent of §XXVIII.13, still to be constructed. *Readout.* $e^\eta$ is a geometric transport factor; its reading as a frequency ratio needs the complex relative transport and detector readout of Part XXVII's open problem 1.

## XXVIII.15 The Berger fibration-selection theorem, the frozen class scale recovered, and the descent to the Berry potential [T/V/D/O]

**The right-isometry theorem [T/V].** The Berger metric on $S^3 = SU(2)$ is left-invariant with inner product $g_\lambda = {\rm diag}(1,1,\lambda^2)$ at the identity, $\lambda\neq1$. Right multiplication by a unit quaternion $h$ acts on the left-invariant frame by ${\rm Ad}_{h^{-1} }$ and is an isometry iff ${\rm Ad}_h^Tg_\lambda{\rm Ad}_h = g_\lambda$; since the eigenvalue $\lambda^2$ is simple, every such ${\rm Ad}_h$ preserves the eigenline $\mathbb R\mathbf e_3$, so ${\rm Ad}_h\mathbf e_3 = \pm\mathbf e_3$ and $h\in U(1)_{\mathbf e_3}\cup\mathbf jU(1)_{\mathbf e_3} = \mathrm{Pin}(2)$ (checked: the circle $e^{t\mathbf e_3}$ and the coset $e^{t\mathbf e_3}\mathbf j$ are isometries, ${\rm Ad}_{\mathbf j}\mathbf e_3 = -\mathbf e_3$, rotations about other axes are not, and none of $2\times10^4$ random unit quaternions is one). *For $\lambda\neq1$ the right-isometry group of the Berger metric is $\mathrm{Pin}(2) = U(1)_{\mathbf e_3}\cup\mathbf jU(1)_{\mathbf e_3}$, its connected component is $U(1)_{\mathbf e_3}$, and the unique right-isometric Hopf-circle action has the unoriented axis $[\mathbf e_3]$* — a conditional uniqueness theorem replacing v32.22's "right-invariant under exactly that $U(1)$": the invariance group is one component larger, the extra component reverses the axis, and the axis it selects is unoriented, which is the sign-line result of §XXVIII.14 arising from the arena's isometries. The condition is *right-isometric Hopf-circle action*; under it the pair's separation, mean and normal axes (at $60^\circ$ from $\mathbf e_3$ along the fold family) are not competing quotient constructions. At $\lambda = 1$ every ${\rm Ad}_h$ is an isometry, the eigenvalue degenerates, all right-Hopf directions are symmetry-equivalent and the selector vanishes — the round arena's $\mathbb{RP}^2$ of fibrations, now explained as the symmetric point of a symmetry-breaking selector that refers at no stage to the scale. Whether the frozen rendering *requires* the physical Hopf quotient to be isometric is the question that decides whether this settles the Berger selection: the rendering selector of §XXVI.2 and the Berger lens of §XXVII.1 use $\pi_{\mathbf e_3}$ throughout, so the requirement is consistent with the frozen construction and is not yet derived from it; recorded as the theorem target, with the orientation sign a separate open item.

**The RMS diagnostic converged, and the directional law's correction [V].** v32.22's eleven-to-thirteen percent excess of $\langle\eta^2\rangle$ over $\tfrac{\pi^2}3\sin^2\tfrac\delta2$ was finite-sample error of sixty random axes: with deterministic Fibonacci quadrature ($n = 50$ and $200$, $\langle(\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m)^2\rangle = 0.3333$ on the grid) the ratio is $1.0016$–$1.0019$ at $\delta = 0.1$ and $1.0174$–$1.0177$ at $\delta = 0.3$. The residual two percent at $\delta = 0.3$ is the directional law's own correction, measured separately: $(\eta_{\mathbf m}-C\,\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m)/(C\,\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m) = (0.102\pm0.008)\,\delta^2$ at $\mathbf m = \mathbf e$ and $0.110\,\delta^2$ at an oblique axis, for $\delta = 0.05$–$0.3$ — quadratic, not quartic (R17), and the one-percent agreement of the earlier eight-axis test at $\delta = 0.3$ was this term. The averaged values are now [V] converged.

**The domain of the section, and the two sign reversals [T/V].** The pair-to-tube map is defined where the projected members are nonantipodal, so for a fixed pair the section's domain is $\mathcal U_\gamma = \{[\mathbf m]: \pi_{\mathbf m}\gamma_+(s)\neq-\pi_{\mathbf m}\gamma_-(s)\ \forall s\}$, and the zero theorem applies when $\mathcal U_\gamma = \mathbb{RP}^2$. Checked over Fibonacci grids of axes: the minimum of $n_+\cdot n_-$ along the path ranges over $[+0.980,+0.995]$, $[+0.825,+0.953]$, $[-0.029,+0.683]$ for the round pair at $\delta = 0.1$, $0.3$, $0.8$ and over $[+0.538,+0.737]$, $[+0.979,+0.989]$ for the Berger pair at $\lambda = 0.79$, $0.802$ — no axis produces an antipodal passage in any tested case, so $\mathcal U_\gamma = \mathbb{RP}^2$ for all of them and the signed-scale section must vanish somewhere; for the leading-order round model the zero locus is the projective equator $\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf m = 0$, while the zeros of the full nonlinear section need their own argument. Two independent sign reversals are kept apart: $\mathbf m\to-\mathbf m$ (the fibration's orientation convention) and $(\gamma_+,\gamma_-)\to(\gamma_-,\gamma_+)$ (the pair's ordering) each send $\eta\to-\eta$, and reversing both leaves it fixed; for a fixed ordered pair the sign line over $\mathbb{RP}^2$ suffices, while for an unordered pair the intrinsic scale is twisted by the tensor product of the fibration sign line and the ordering sign line — a distinction to be carried into the history groupoid, where which exchanges are physical equivalences is decided. $\eta^2$ and $|\eta|$ survive both.

**The frozen class scale recovered, with its normalization [T/V].** The frozen §XV.3 defines the scale character of a class as the relative scale of the two conjugate lifts $\widetilde\gamma_\pm = \gamma\pm i\epsilon Y$ of *one* real leg, $\eta_\Xi = 2\epsilon\int\bar F_H(Y,k)\,ds+O(\epsilon^3)$, evaluated over the complex ribbon between the lifts; the pair reading of §XXVIII.14 evaluates one complex history $\Phi(x,v)$ against the real mean. These are the same law in two normalizations, checked on one configuration: the lift $\gamma+iY$ against the real leg gives $\eta_+ = +0.157967$, the conjugate lift $\gamma-iY$ gives $\eta_- = -0.157967$, and the frozen class scale is their difference, $\eta_+-\eta_- = 0.315935 = 2\eta_+$. So the frozen $\epsilon Y$ is the pair reading's half-separation $v$, and with the pair's full separation $J = 2v$,
$$\eta_\Xi = -\int F_H(J,k)\,ds+O(\|J\|^3) = -\Phi_{\rm lune}+O(\|J\|^3),$$
*the frozen class scale is minus the whole Hopf flux through the lune between the projected members at leading order*, the pair reading's $\eta = -\tfrac12\Phi_{\rm lune}$ being half of it; the equality is first-order, as the numbers at $\lambda = 0.8$ show ($2\times0.40028 = 0.80056$ against $0.79623$), and the sign is a convention fixed in §XXVIII.16. The fold pair's class scales in the frozen normalization are therefore $\eta_\Xi = 1.752$, $0.801$, $0.362$, $0.233$ at $\lambda = 0.790$, $0.800$, $0.802$, $0.8023$, i.e. $e^{\eta_\Xi} = 5.77$, $2.23$, $1.44$, $1.26$ — transport factors, not redshifts, and the frozen "no new field" statement is confirmed in the pair reading: the scale is fixed by $F_H$ with no coefficient free. Part XV's exchange-odd class scale and Part XXVIII's pair reading are one construction; what Part XXVIII adds is the explicit assignment of the frozen $Y$ — the pair's projected half-separation — and the demonstration on actual Part XXVII histories.

**The descent to the Berry potential: the step the frozen definitions permit [T/V/O].** In the frozen architecture the canonical space $E$ restricted to a source shell is the Hopf lift $S^3\to S^2$, the middle space is $\mathcal M = E/U(1)_H$, and §XV.3 types the Hopf curvature as basic, $F_H = \pi_H^*\bar F_H$ with $\bar F_H$ a two-form on $\mathcal M$. On a single shell, therefore, the axis sphere of §XXVIII.14 *is* the shell's image in the middle space, and $\bar F_H$ there *is* the Berry curvature of §XXVIII.12 — so the scale of the pair reading is already a flux of the frozen middle-space curvature, by the frozen definitions and nothing more. What the pair reading does not supply by definition is the Weyl one-form $A$ of §XV.1 itself: it supplies the *integral* over a lune. Stokes converts it. Since $F_H = d\beta$ on the shell, the lune flux is the difference of the two members' line integrals of the Berry potential in a common gauge,
$$\eta_\Xi = -\Big(\int_{\gamma_+}\beta-\int_{\gamma_-}\beta\Big),$$
checked on the Berger fold pair at $\lambda = 0.8$ in the northern gauge, which is regular along both members ($\min z = -0.625$): lune flux $-0.79623$, difference of line integrals $-0.79624$. This is the frozen mean-and-difference algebra of §XV.6 made explicit on actual histories: the *mean* of the members' Berry line integrals is what one history sees, a phase; their *difference* is what the pair sees, a scale. A first reading took this as a candidate identification of §XV.1's $A$ along a leg with a Berry potential $\beta$ in a definite gauge; that reading is withdrawn in §XXVIII.16 (R19): $A_{\rm scale} = {\rm Re}\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ vanishes on the real slice while $\beta$ does not, so the Stokes identity is a *Berry-flux representation of the leading class-scale variation*, not a derivation of the Weyl potential; the difference of the members' integrals is gauge-invariant because the endpoint terms cancel, while an open-path integral of $\beta$ needs endpoint frames and a gauge choice is not itself physical, and $\beta$ is not globally defined on the sphere ($\tfrac1{2\pi}\int F_H = 1$), so the northern-gauge identity holds on its patch with the $2\pi$ ambiguity of spanning surfaces handled by the continuously specified narrow ribbon. The descent is thereby advanced one exact step and stopped at four named gaps, in order: (a) the identification of the pair's projected members with the two *legs* of a frozen class and of the half-separation with §XV.3's Jacobi $Y$ — the Jacobi identification, open; (b) the relation of ${\rm Re}\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ on the displaced complex history to §XV.1's affine $A$ on the middle space — the descent proper, with $A|_{TS^2} = 0$ as a constraint it must respect — open; (c) the non-angular components, $\bar F_H(\partial_{\rm mer},k)$ of 20.3, which the shell calculation cannot see and which carry the twin-parity sign rule — open; (d) the readout: §XV.1 gives length transport $e^{-\int A}$ along a $\nabla^\pm$-parallel field and hence a frequency factor $e^{+\int A}$, but that $e^{\eta_\Xi}$ is the ratio a detector measures is Part XXVII's open problem 1 — open. The chain *physical pair $\to$ selected axis $\to$ complex Berry transport $\to$ middle-space Weyl transport $\to$ observable* now has its first two arrows constructed on the Berger arena (the axis by the isometry theorem under the isometric requirement, the transport by the pair reading), its third arrow carried to the Berry-flux representation of the leading scale on a single shell, and its fourth not at all.

## XXVIII.16 The Jacobi test and its magnetic obstruction: real arena variations, Hopf projection, and curvature-driven scale [T/V/D/O]

**Two corrections carried into §XXVIII.15 [R].** First, the Berry-potential identification is withdrawn (R19): on the real axis sphere $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}|_{S^2} = i\beta$, so the scale form $A_{\rm scale} = {\rm Re}\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ vanishes on $TS^2$ — the firewall of §XXVIII.13 — while $\beta$ does not and has curvature $F_H\neq0$; the two have different curvatures on the real slice, $d(A_{\rm scale}|_{TS^2}) = 0$ against $d\beta = F_H$, and no gauge makes them one connection. The Stokes identity stands as what it is: a difference of two real Berry integrals *represents* the leading scale variation of a complex history, without the Berry potential becoming a dilation connection; the scale form is ${\rm Re}\,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ on the displaced complex history, not $\beta$ on the real leg, and the candidate for §XV.1's $A$ along a leg is withdrawn with it. Second, the recovery of the frozen class scale is first-order, not exact (R20): $\eta_\Xi = -\Phi_{\rm lune}+O(\|J\|^3)$ — visible in the manuscript's own numbers at $\lambda = 0.8$, $2\times0.40028 = 0.80056$ against $0.79623$ — with the convention dictionary now explicit: $F_H(Y,k) = -F_H(k,Y)$, so with $F_H = \tfrac12x\cdot(dx\wedge dx)$ oriented by the outward normal, ${\rm Hol} = \exp\oint\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ and the lift $\gamma+i\epsilon Y$, ${\rm Re}\log{\rm Hol} = -\epsilon\int F_H(Y,k)\,ds$, the relative scale of $\gamma+i\epsilon Y$ against $\gamma-i\epsilon Y$ is $-2\epsilon\int F_H(Y,k)\,ds$, and the frozen "$+2$" is the opposite argument order; magnitudes agree exactly, the sign is a convention to be fixed once with the ordering of the pair. The referee's wording is adopted: *the Part XV conjugate-lift scale and the Part XXVIII pair scale have the same first-variation structure, with a factor of two from relative transport and an orientation convention to be fixed; the real Hopf-lune flux supplies their leading-order value, finite separation introduces higher-order corrections.* And "converged" refers to the angular quadrature, not to every numerical component.

**The exact domain criterion [T/V].** For histories $q_\pm(s)\in SU(2)$ with relative quaternion $g(s) = q_+^{-1}q_-$, the projections under the axis $\mathbf m$ satisfy $n_+\cdot n_- = \mathbf m\cdot{\rm Ad}_g\mathbf m = \cos\Theta+(1-\cos\Theta)(\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf a)^2$ (Rodrigues), so $\min_{\mathbf m}(n_+\cdot n_-) = 2({\rm Re}\,g)^2-1$ and the projections are antipodal for some axis iff ${\rm Re}\,g = 0$ — the two points of $S^3$ at separation $\pi/2$. The midpoint assignment is defined for every axis throughout the pair iff ${\rm Re}(q_+^{-1}q_-)\neq0$ for every $s$, a single scalar function replacing the grid. Checked: $\min_s|{\rm Re}\,g| = 0.9950$, $0.9553$, $0.6967$, $0.0707$ for the round pair at $\delta = 0.1$, $0.3$, $0.8$, $1.5$ (exact minima of $n_+\cdot n_-$ over all axes $+0.980$, $+0.825$, $-0.029$, $-0.990$; the sampled $-0.029$ of v32.23 was the exact value) and $0.8770$, $0.9741$, $0.9947$, $0.9978$ for the Berger family — all nonzero, so $\mathcal U_\gamma = \mathbb{RP}^2$ for every tested pair holds as a theorem [T], and the zero theorem applies to all of them.

**The Jacobi test, and its result [T/V].** The referee's strong failure test: does the projected half-separation $v(s)$ satisfy the Jacobi equation along the mean history $x(s)$ on the axis sphere, $D^2v/ds^2+R(v,k)k = 0$ with $R(v,k)k = |k|^2v-(v\cdot k)k$ on the unit sphere, with $x$ itself a geodesic? It does not. On the round arena with the separation along the fiber axis — the configuration that carries the scale — the mean curve's geodesic defect is $0.02$, $0.18$, $1.56$ and the relative Jacobi residual $0.64$, $0.65$, $0.71$ at $\delta = 0.1$, $0.3$, $0.8$; with an oblique axis the defects are $3.8$ and the residuals $0.4$–$0.5$; on the Berger fold pair the mean-curve defect is $5$ and the residual $0.44$ — order one, independent of the opening, not a discretization effect. The reason is exact and was verified separately: the Hopf projection of a great circle of $S^3$ with initial velocity $w$ is a circle of geodesic curvature $\kappa_g = c/\sqrt{1-c^2}$, $c = w\cdot\mathbf m$ its fiber component (checked to four digits at $c = 0$, $0.3$, $0.6$) — a geodesic of the axis sphere only if the geodesic of the arena is horizontal. The control confirms it from the other side: for a *horizontal* pair, both initial velocities perpendicular to the fiber axis, the projections are great circles, the mean is a geodesic and $v$ *is* a Jacobi field (residuals $2\times10^{-3}$ and $2\times10^{-2}$ at $\delta = 0.1$, $0.3$, the $O(\delta^2)$ floor of the mean-curve construction) — and the scale is zero, since the separation is horizontal. Upstairs on the arena itself the pair's half-separation $W(s) = \tfrac12(q_+-q_-)^\perp$ *is* a Jacobi field along the mean geodesic (residual $1.6\times10^{-2}$ at $\delta = 0.3$, the same floor), as the frozen §XV.3 assumes of its $Y$. The statement these facts first suggested — that $v$ is Jacobi on the axis sphere *exactly when* it carries no scale — is too strong, and is replaced below by the referee's counterexample and the magnetic deviation equation (R21); what the facts establish is that the pair reading's displacement is the Hopf projection of the arena's (infinitesimally) Jacobi half-separation, that horizontality of the pair is sufficient for the projection to be an ordinary Jacobi field, and that in the scale-carrying configurations the members have a fiber component, their projections are small circles, the mean is not a geodesic and $v$ is not Jacobi.

**What this decides [D].** The midpoint construction cannot be identified with the frozen §XV.3 imaginary Jacobi variation *on the axis sphere*: the pair's half-separation is (infinitesimally) Jacobi on the arena, and it is the arena pair — not its projection — that carries the Jacobi structure. The scale is a property of the arena pair read through the fibration, $\eta = -\tfrac12\int F_H(\pi_*W,\pi_*k)\,ds$ with $W$ Jacobi upstairs, and the frozen formula $\eta_\Xi = 2\epsilon\int\bar F_H(Y,k)\,ds$ evaluates $\bar F_H$ on horizontal lifts of $k,Y\in T\mathcal M$ — but §XV.3's $Y$ carries the Jacobi structure of the *null history in the middle space*, not of the arena, a distinction stated correctly at the end of this section (R23); so the pair reading and the frozen class scale agree on how the scale is read (through $\bar F_H$) while the identification of their Jacobi fields remains the intertwiner to construct. And the fiber component that carries the scale is the component the Berger squashing distinguishes: on the Berger arena the isometry theorem of §XXVIII.15 selects the fibration, the fold pair's members have a fiber component along it ($60^\circ$ from the separation axis), and the scale is nonzero for that reason — the three results close on one another. What the test does not decide is the physical identification of the arena pair with a class's two legs, which remains the Jacobi identification in its correct form: *is the frozen $Y$ the half-separation of an admissible pair of arena histories?* — now a question about the arena, where §XXVII's admissibility structure lives, and no longer about the axis sphere.

**The counterexample, and the theorem replaced [R/T/V].** The "iff" of the preceding paragraph is false in one direction (R21), and the referee's counterexample proves it: on the round arena with axis $\mathbf e_3$ and initial directions $\mathbf u_\pm = \cos a\,\mathbf e_3\pm\sin a\,\mathbf e_1$, the projected midpoint is *constant*, $x(s) = \mathbf e_3$ (checked to machine precision), the half-separation is $v(s) = \sin a[\cos a(1-\cos2s)\mathbf e_1-\sin2s\,\mathbf e_2]$ (checked), the Jacobi equation along a constant curve reduces to $D^2v/ds^2 = 0$ while $D^2v/ds^2|_0 = 4\sin a\cos a\,\mathbf e_1\neq0$ (checked, $1.68\,\mathbf e_1$ at $a = 0.5$), and yet the complex scale vanishes identically, $\eta = 0$ ($z_3$ real and $z_{1,2}$ imaginary along the tube curve make $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ purely imaginary). Zero scale does not imply a projected Jacobi field. What survives is one direction: *horizontality of the family is sufficient for the projected variation to be an ordinary Jacobi field at the infinitesimal level*; vanishing integrated scale is not. The finite half-separation is also only infinitesimally Jacobi upstairs (R22): the exact Jacobi field is $W_0 = \partial_aq|_{a=0}$ of a family of geodesics, the finite symmetric difference is $\epsilon W_0+O(\epsilon^3)$, the normalized midpoint need not be affinely parametrized, and the residuals reported upstairs ($1.6\times10^{-2}$) are these corrections and not noise; and two isolated geodesics joining the same endpoints — the Berger fold pair away from the fold — need not belong to a continuous family joining them, so the finite branch separation approximates the emerging null mode near the fold and is not an exact endpoint-vanishing Jacobi field away from it.

**The magnetic reduction: Hopf projections of arena geodesics [T/V].** The failure has an exact and more informative form. On the round $S^3$ take the great circle $q(s) = e^{s\mathbf w}$, the axis $\mathbf m$, the conserved fiber momentum $c = \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf m$, the projection $n = q\mathbf mq^{-1}$ with $k = \dot n$ and $\mathcal J$ the $90^\circ$ rotation in $T_nS^2$. Then
$$D_sk = 2c\,\mathcal Jk,$$
the *magnetic geodesic equation* on the axis sphere (checked: residual $4\times10^{-7}$ at $c = 0.3$, $0.6$; $|k| = 2\sqrt{1-c^2}$), ordinary geodesic motion at $c = 0$ and, at $c\neq0$, a Lorentz-type force whose strength is the fiber momentum — the equation behind the geodesic curvature $\kappa_g = c/\sqrt{1-c^2}$ of §XXVIII.16's first paragraph. For a smooth family $q(s,a)$ of arena geodesics with arena Jacobi field $W = \partial_aq$ and projected variation $V = \partial_an$, differentiating the magnetic equation in $a$ gives the *magnetic deviation equation*
$$D_s^2V+R(V,k)k = 2c\,\mathcal JD_sV+2(\partial_ac)\,\mathcal Jk,$$
the correct replacement for the quotient Jacobi equation: the projected arena Jacobi field solves the *linearized magnetic geodesic equation*, inhomogeneous whenever the family changes its fiber momentum, even if the central history is horizontal. The referee's analytic case was reproduced exactly: central direction $\mathbf e_1$ varied toward $\mathbf e_3$, central projection $n = \cos2s\,\mathbf e_3-\sin2s\,\mathbf e_2$ a great circle, $V = (1-\cos2s)\mathbf e_1$ vanishing at both ends, ordinary Jacobi residual $D^2V+R(V,k)k = 4\mathbf e_1$, and $2(\partial_ac)\mathcal Jk = 4\mathbf e_1$ with $\partial_ac = 1$ — the magnetic deviation residual $4\times10^{-7}$, and the two general cases ($c_0 = 0.296$, varied toward $\mathbf e_3$ and toward $\mathbf e_2$) give $5\times10^{-7}$ and $2\times10^{-6}$. And the scale: $\int_0^\pi F_H(V,k)\,ds = -\pi$ for that family — *the very variation that fails the ordinary Jacobi equation produces the first-order scale*, which is the relationship that replaces the withdrawn mutual exclusion: the departure from ordinary geodesic deviation and the scale response are both governed by the Hopf curvature, through the fiber momentum and its change across the family.

**The Berger analogue: one formula for both arenas [T/V].** The Berger geodesic with left-invariant initial velocity $v$ is $\exp_\lambda(tv) = e^{t(v+\kappa\mathbf e_3)}e^{-t\kappa\mathbf e_3}$, $\kappa = (\lambda^2-1)v_3$ (§XXVII.2), and the right factor fixes $\mathbf e_3$ under the adjoint action; so its Hopf projection with axis $\mathbf e_3$ is *exactly* the projection of the round great circle $e^{t\mathbf w}$ with $\mathbf w = v+\kappa\mathbf e_3$ (checked to $6\times10^{-16}$). The Berger projection is therefore a magnetic geodesic of the *round* axis sphere with effective fiber momentum
$$c_{\rm eff} = \frac{\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf e_3}{|\mathbf w|} = \frac{\lambda^2v_3}{|v+\kappa\mathbf e_3|},$$
the squashing rescaling the vertical momentum by $\lambda^2$ and the speed, and entering nowhere else (checked: magnetic residual $1.4\times10^{-7}$). The reduction is therefore the same on both arenas — the Pin(2) isometry of §XXVIII.15 is exactly what conserves $c_{\rm eff}$, and the selected fibration is the one for which the reduction holds — and the magnetic deviation equation, with $c|\mathbf w|$ in place of $c$ for the arena's parametrization, holds on the fold-pair family itself: for $v(a) = \bar v+a\,\delta v$ through the pair at $\lambda = 0.8$ ($c_0 = 0.493$, $|\mathbf w| = 5.13$, $\partial_a(c|\mathbf w|) = 0.255$) the ordinary Jacobi residual is $0.45$ and the magnetic deviation residual $1.8\times10^{-5}$; its first-order scale $\int F_H(V,k)\,dt = -0.402$ matches the finite pair reading $\eta = 0.400 = -\tfrac12\Phi_{\rm lune}$ at $a = \pm1$. The theorem, on both arenas: *Hopf projections of arena geodesics are magnetic geodesics of the round axis sphere with conserved fiber momentum $c_{\rm eff}$; their projected variations obey the magnetic deviation equation exactly; the inhomogeneous source is the change of fiber momentum across the family; variations within the horizontal family satisfy the ordinary projected Jacobi equation, and in general the departure from it is governed by $c$, $\delta c$ and the Hopf geometry* (the "iff" first written here was too strong, R24). The real-geometric chain the referee set out is thereby constructed on both arenas — arena geodesics and Jacobi variations $\to$ conserved fiber momentum $\to$ magnetic projected-history equation $\to$ Berry curvature and scale variation — with the complex displacement no longer assigned by hand but produced by the projection of the arena's own variation.

**Part XV's Jacobi field, stated correctly [D/O].** v32.24's closing sentence — that the frozen §XV.3 never required $Y$ to be Jacobi on the quotient, only upstairs — was too broad (R23). §XV.3 does not require $Y$ to be Jacobi for the round metric on the axis sphere; it does require the Jacobi structure *along the real null history in the middle-space geometry* $\mathcal M$, and evaluates the basic curvature on horizontal lifts of $k,Y\in T\mathcal M$ with the endpoint-conjugacy condition. The Part XXVII arena is a Riemannian or Berger $S^3$; the Part XV history is a null history in $\mathcal M$; these are different assertions, and the fact that $W$ is Jacobi on the arena does not by itself make it the $Y$ of §XV.3. The intertwiner between the two history variations is therefore still required, and the magnetic deviation equation is a component of it — the equation a projected arena variation satisfies, against which the §XV.3 requirement can be compared — not the intertwiner itself. The Berger statement that ${\rm Re}(q_+^{-1}q_-)$ never vanishes is kept at [V], the round values $\min|{\rm Re}\,g| = |\cos\delta|$ being analytic ($0.9950$, $0.9553$, $0.6967$, $0.0707$ as reported) while the Berger minima are numerical without a certified bound; the criterion itself is [T]. The next test is the one the referee names: whether the real history dynamics themselves produce the complex transport structure — whether the magnetic reduction, transported into §XV.3's null-history geometry, yields its conjugate lifts — rather than whether that structure can represent their separation.

## XXVIII.17 Real Routh reduction and the magnetic-to-arena Jacobi intertwiner [T/V/D/O]

**One correction carried into §XXVIII.16 [R].** The closing sentence — that the ordinary Jacobi equation holds iff the family is horizontal with $c\equiv0$ — was too strong (R24). The magnetic deviation equation gives the exact condition: $D_s^2V+R(V,k)k = 0$ iff $c\,\mathcal JD_sV+(\delta c)\,\mathcal Jk = 0$; $c = 0$ with $\delta c = 0$ is sufficient and not shown necessary, and a horizontal central history with $\delta c\neq0$ is still forced, as the analytic example shows. The theorem reads: *Hopf projections of round and Berger arena geodesics obey the magnetic-geodesic equation and projected geodesic variations obey its exact linearization; variations within the horizontal geodesic family satisfy the ordinary projected Jacobi equation; in general the departure from it is governed by the vertical momentum, its variation across the family, and the Hopf geometry.* And the complex displacement, though now available from the arena variation, still enters the Grauert tube through the chosen pair-to-complex-history prescription; that physical identification is not uniquely derived.

**Step A: Berry curvature and magnetic motion from one real action [T/V].** The Berger metric on $SU(2)$ in Hopf coordinates is
$$g_\lambda = \tfrac14\,\pi^*g_{S^2}+\lambda^2(d\psi-\beta)^2,\qquad d\beta = F_H = \tfrac12\omega_{S^2},$$
checked pointwise: along random tangent vectors $|dn|^2 = 4(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$ to $6\times10^{-10}$ (the Hopf map doubles angles, so the base is $S^2(\tfrac12)$ and the horizontal part of the metric is $\tfrac14\pi^*g_{S^2}$ for the unit sphere), and $\sigma_3 = d\psi-\beta$ is the left-invariant fiber form with $d\sigma_3 = -2\sigma_1\wedge\sigma_2 = -\tfrac12\pi^*\omega_{S^2}$ by Maurer–Cartan — the Hopf connection *is* the third left-invariant form, with the Berry curvature its structure constant. The fiber coordinate $\psi$ is cyclic in the geodesic Lagrangian $L = \tfrac12g_\lambda(\dot x,\dot x)$, so its momentum $b = \lambda^2(\dot\psi-\beta(\dot n)) = \lambda^2\sigma_3(\dot q)$ is conserved (checked: $\sigma_3$ constant to $4\times10^{-11}$ along a Berger geodesic, $b = \lambda^2v_3$), and Routh reduction at fixed $b$ gives the reduced Lagrangian
$$L_b = \tfrac18|\dot n|^2-b\,\beta(\dot n)-\frac{b^2}{2\lambda^2},$$
whose Euler–Lagrange equations are $\tfrac14D_t\dot n = -b\,F_H(\cdot,\dot n)$, i.e. $D_t\dot n = 2b\,\mathcal J\dot n$ — the magnetic geodesic equation of §XXVIII.16, now *derived from a real variational principle*. Checked three ways: the magnetic coefficient fitted from a projected Berger geodesic's own data is $\mu = +0.76800 = 2\lambda^2\sigma_3$ with residual $2\times10^{-9}$; the Euler–Lagrange equations of $L_b$ integrated in Cartesian form reproduce the projected Berger geodesic to $1.8\times10^{-4}$ (the finite-difference precision of the initial velocity), against $0.49$ for $b = 0$ and $0.84$ for $-b$; and the reduction is gauge-invariant, since $\beta\to\beta+d\chi$ with $\psi\to\psi+\chi$ leaves $\sigma_3$ and $b$ fixed and changes $L_b$ by the total derivative $-b\dot\chi$. (A first spherical-coordinate form of the $\phi$-equation carried a sign error and was discarded; the Cartesian form is unambiguous.) The consequence the referee wanted is now a theorem: the term responsible for magnetic motion is $-b\,\beta(\dot n)$, whose curvature is exactly the Berry curvature of the complex transport, so *one real Berger metric and its geodesic action yield, through one connection $\beta$, both the real magnetic motion $D_tk = 2b\mathcal Jk$ and the complex phase–scale transport $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C} = {\rm hol.ext.}(i\beta)$* — derived from the same real connection, not matched after separate calculations. Established geometry within the chosen arena, not a new law; and now a variational foundation for the bridge.

**Step B: the rotating frame [T].** Writing the deviation equation with the conserved momentum, $D_t^2V+\mathcal R_kV = 2b\,\mathcal JD_tV+2(\delta b)\mathcal Jk$, the gyroscopic term is removed by the orthogonal frame $U_b$ with $D_tU_b = b\,\mathcal JU_b$: since $\mathcal J$ commutes with $U_b$ and $D(U_bZ) = U_b(DZ+b\mathcal JZ)$, the substitution $V = U_bZ$ gives
$$D_t^2Z+\big(U_b^{-1}\mathcal R_kU_b+b^2I\big)Z = 2(\delta b)\,U_b^{-1}\mathcal Jk,$$
with the symmetric effective tidal operator $\mathcal R_{\rm eff} = U_b^{-1}\mathcal R_kU_b+b^2I$ — homogeneous, and of ordinary geodesic-deviation form, iff $\delta b = 0$. The deviation equation itself was confirmed on the round family at $10^{-7}$ in §XXVIII.16 and the frame transformation is pure algebra; on the transverse screen the effective tidal eigenvalue is $|k|^2+b^2$ with $b = c$ on the unit-speed round arena (the frame rotates at half the cyclotron coefficient), i.e. $4(1-c^2)+c^2 = 4-3c^2$: $4.00$, $3.73$, $2.92$ at $c = 0$, $0.3$, $0.6$ — the first version of this sentence substituted $b = 2c$ and claimed the constant $4$, which is withdrawn (R26, §XXVIII.18); O'Neill's $K_{\rm base} = 1+3|A_XY|^2 = 4$ is the curvature of the Hopf base in its submersion metric, not the effective tidal eigenvalue of the reduced variation equation. The sharp choice the referee set stands: either the admissible variation class preserves $b$, or the physical state carries $\delta b$ as relational data; it is to be decided by Part XXVII's admissibility rules and not chosen.

**Step C: the comparison with the frozen physical screen system, and the failure of the identity intertwiner [T/V].** The frozen §XIII.10 fixes the physical system on the round benchmark: the static metric $-N^2dt^2+\phi^4g_{\rm ref}$ has Fermat metric $\bar h = (\phi^4/N^2)g_{\rm ref}$, rays are its geodesics, the screen Jacobi equation on the bare round arena is $J''+J/\ell^2 = 0$, and the first conjugate point is the antipode at $L = \pi\ell$ — the physical optical tidal operator is $\mathcal R_{\rm phys} = 1$ (unit $\ell$) on the two-screen, along the *arena* geodesic. For the horizontal round family ($c = 0$) the projected system has $\mathcal R_{\rm eff}^\perp = 4$ and first zero at $s = \pi/2$ — a horizontal-sector result, not a property of every fixed-momentum family (R27, §XXVIII.18: $V(\pi/2) = 2c\,\partial_a\mathbf w$ vanishes only at $c = 0$, while $V(\pi) = 0$ for every $c$). In that benchmark the decisive invariants disagree by a factor of two in the affine parameter, and the discrepancy is exact and explained: the Hopf projection of a great circle closes at the base antipode at $s = \pi/2$, so the projections of two arena geodesics from $q$ re-cross there (the horizontal family's projected variation vanishes at $s = 1.5708$, checked) while the arena geodesics themselves are separated along the fiber ($0.2000$ apart in $S^3$ for $a = \pm0.1$, on one Hopf fiber) and the arena Jacobi field has no interior zero. *The projected system's conjugate point is a crossing of projections, not of arena histories.* An intertwiner $\mathcal I_\gamma:V\mapsto Y$ that is the identity on the transverse screen with the same affine parameter therefore fails the focusing test, as the referee's protocol required it be allowed to; the obstruction is recorded, and no transport map is defined to force agreement.

**The intertwiner that the failure forces [T/V].** What the projection loses is the fiber component, and it is recoverable. For a family $q(s,a) = \exp(s\,\mathbf w(a))$ of round arena geodesics, the Jacobi field in left-invariant components is
$$q^{-1}\partial_aq = \int_0^s{\rm Ad}_{\exp(-t\mathbf w)}(\delta\mathbf w)\,dt$$
(checked to $3\times10^{-5}$ against the numerical field), whose vertical component on the round arena is
$$W_v(s) = \tfrac12(\delta c)\sin2s-\tfrac12\big((\mathbf w\times\delta\mathbf w)\cdot\mathbf e_3\big)(1-\cos2s),\qquad \delta c = \delta\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf e_3,$$
checked to $10^{-11}$ on the referee's family ($W_v = \tfrac12\cos a_0\sin2s$). A first guess, $W_v = \int(\delta b+\beta(V))$, was wrong and is discarded; the fiber component is governed by the Lie-algebraic transport of the velocity variation, not by a line integral of the connection on the projected variation. The horizontal part is the projection's: $V = \pi_*W_h$ with $|V| = 2|W_h|$ (ratio $2.0000$, checked), $\pi_*$ an isomorphism on horizontal vectors, so $V$ determines $W_h$, hence $\delta\mathbf w_h$ from its initial growth, while $\delta c$ is the vertical part of $\delta\mathbf w$; together they give $\delta\mathbf w$ and thereby the entire $W$. *The pair $(V,\delta c)$ — the magnetic variation and the vertical-momentum variation, exactly the data the referee named — is a complete, lossless encoding of the arena Jacobi field, and the map $(V,\delta c)\mapsto W$ is forced by the geometry, not chosen.* This is the arena reconstruction (the intertwiner's arena-sector part, not the physical intertwiner): not the identity on the screen, but the restoration of the fiber component from $\delta c$, after which the arena Jacobi field — which coincides with the optical Jacobi structure in the bare round benchmark of §XIII.10, whose conjugate point is the antipode, and not automatically in the physical Fermat metric with its lapse and conformal factor — is recovered exactly; this is an *arena reconstruction*, not an intertwiner to the physical Lorentzian null-history system.
